about: Maps three.js APIs to their null3D equivalents. Each entry gives a status and a docs page ID.

statusLegend.direct: Same concept; the call or option changes name only.
statusLegend.changed: Supported, with a different API or pattern. Follow the note.
statusLegend.manual: Must be rewritten by hand, for example GLSL shaders or render hooks.
statusLegend.unsupported: null3D has no equivalent. Use the workaround in the note.

entries.target: createEngine({ canvas, sketch }) on the page; scene code moves to sketch.ts inside defineSketch()
entries.notes: The engine picks WebGPU or WebGL2 itself. `antialias: true` becomes `createEngine({ antialias: 'msaa' })`, and `false` becomes `'none'`. `alpha: true` becomes `transparent: true`, and `powerPreference` keeps its name.
entries.details: Without `antialias`, the quality preset picks FXAA on Low and MSAA 4x from Medium up. The default `powerPreference` is `'high-performance'`.

entries.target: createEngine({ maxPixelRatio }) and the quality presets; quality.set({ maxPixelRatio }) in the sketch
entries.notes: The engine sizes the canvas to its CSS size times the screen's pixel ratio, up to the quality preset's cap. The option replaces the cap, and quality.set changes it during play.

entries.three: renderer.setSize / window resize handler / camera.aspect + updateProjectionMatrix
entries.target: Automatic
entries.notes: The engine follows the canvas's CSS size. Perspective cameras, and orthographic cameras made with a height, follow its aspect ratio in every frame. Delete resize handlers and updateProjectionMatrix calls.

entries.target: onUpdate(dt) returned from defineSketch()
entries.notes: The engine renders every frame by itself; never call a render function. Per-frame logic goes in onUpdate, camera-follow logic in onLateUpdate.

entries.target: castShadows: true on the light; the shadowFilter quality setting sets the filter
entries.notes: PCFShadowMap and PCFSoftShadowMap become the shadowFilter setting: 3 x 3 or 5 x 5 texels, by preset. quality.set({ shadowFilter }) changes it during play.

entries.target: None; the shadowFilter quality setting chooses the filter
entries.notes: null3D filters every shadow with PCF, a 3 x 3 or 5 x 5 kernel chosen by the shadowFilter quality setting. It draws no basic or variance shadow map.

entries.three: renderer.toneMapping (ACESFilmic, AgX, Neutral, Reinhard, Cineon, Custom, Linear) / toneMappingExposure
entries.target: post.set({ toneMapping: 'agx' | 'agx-punchy' | 'neutral' | 'aces' | 'none' | curveWgsl, exposure })
entries.notes: The engine default is `agx-punchy`, and three.js defaults to none, so a port of a scene with none sets `toneMapping: 'none'`. A port keeps its curve: AgX becomes `'agx'`, ACES `'aces'` and Neutral `'neutral'`. Copy `toneMappingExposure` to `exposure`, but keep `exposure` at 1 for NoToneMapping, which ignores it.
entries.details:
`ReinhardToneMapping` and `CineonToneMapping` become the `reinhard` and `cineon` curves of `@null3d/three-compat`. `CustomToneMapping` becomes a custom tone curve: `post.set({ toneMapping: wgsl })`. The WGSL declares `fn toneCurve(color: vec3f) -> vec3f`. Leave out the curve's multiply by `toneMappingExposure`, because the color arrives exposed.

The curves use three.js's formulas. `'none'` applies the exposure, as `LinearToneMapping` does. null3D multiplies the exposure into each light rather than into the finished picture. This gives the same image, and bloom's threshold keeps its meaning. A scene in real units sets `ev100` instead, and exposure then acts as exposure compensation. At `ev100` 15, background and unlit colors draw black unless their values are in real units too.

A custom curve needs HDR color, as bloom does. Compatibility mode then draws in HDR color with FXAA. A device without an HDR target keeps the built-in curve.

entries.target: Nothing to do
entries.notes: Output is sRGB from a linear working space, as in three.js r152+ defaults. Hex colors are sRGB, and `[r, g, b]` arrays are linear, as three.js reads them. Delete the output and color management lines.
entries.details: The final pass encodes sRGB and dithers. three.js dithers only materials with `dithering: true`, so delete that option. The difference is at most one step of an 8-bit color.

entries.target: debug.stats(true), or createEngine({ stats: true }) on the page; debug.frameStats() for numbers
entries.notes: The overlay shows frame rates, per-thread CPU time, draw calls, the GPU tier and the preset. Click it for a card of thread and GPU times, objects drawn and memory. In the sketch, `debug.frameStats()` also gives the textures' GPU bytes, their budget and their dropped mip levels.
entries.details:
`debug.stats(true)`, `createEngine({ stats: true })`, `engine.stats(true)` or `?stats` turns the overlay on. It sits at the canvas's top right, or at its bottom right with `{ corner: 'bottom-right' }`. Its header shows the frame rate.

The card shows each thread's and the GPU's time against the target frame rate. It also shows the memory of the engine, the GPU's textures and buffers, the heap and the page.

Triangles count every pass, shadow maps included, as `renderer.info.render.triangles` does. Objects count the instances of each draw, so an object counts once per pass that draws it. Each part of a mesh with several materials counts once, as each part is a mesh of its own in three.js. `engine.measure(seconds)` on the page gives percentiles of CPU and GPU time, and memory. `@null3d/engine/stats` shows a three.js page's own figures in the same panel, with `StatsPanel`, or as text, with `statsText`.

entries.target: quality.textureMemory; textures.memoryBytes; the quality setting textureMemoryMiB; debug.frameStats().gpuTextureBytes and gpuBufferBytes
entries.notes: three.js counts the textures it holds and sets no byte budget. null3D reports the textures' GPU bytes and holds them under the preset's budget. Past it, textures from files drop their largest mip levels, which load again when room returns.
entries.details: `debug.frameStats()` gives the bytes of every GPU texture and buffer that the engine holds. Render targets and shadow maps are included.

entries.target: await scene.warmUp() before hiding the loading screen
entries.notes: The first frame waits for its pipelines. warmUp resolves once every pipeline that the scene needs is built, hidden objects included, so warm up a later loading stage before you show it.

entries.target: scene.setBackground('#rrggbb' | texture | environment | cube map | { sky }, options)
entries.notes: A texture background fills the view behind every object and stretches to its shape. An environment or cube map surrounds the scene, as a PMREM texture or CubeTexture does. For an exact page color, set `toneMapping: 'none'` or use `createEngine({ transparent: true })` over CSS.
entries.details: Exposure and tone mapping change the background, as in three.js's `WebGPURenderer`. `WebGLRenderer` draws a background color, and an sRGB background texture, without them. `setClearColor(color, 0)` on an alpha canvas becomes `transparent: true` with no background.

entries.target: createEngine({ canvas })
entries.notes: Create the canvas in HTML or in page.ts and pass it in. The engine hands it to the render worker.

entries.target: await engine.capture() on the page
entries.notes: Resolves with a PNG Blob of the next frame that the engine draws. Tests read pixels with engine.captureFrame() instead.

entries.target: const pass = render.addPass({ kind: 'scene', camera, writes: 'myTexture', size: [width, height] }); materials.unlit({ map: textures.fromPass(pass) })
entries.notes: Declare a pass and let the render graph order it, run it while its texture shows, and plan its memory. A pass never draws objects that show its own texture. Scene passes draw point and spot lights and the background, but no ambient occlusion.
entries.details:
The texture holds linear color after the exposure. It is upright, with `v = 0` at the bottom, as three.js's render target texture. A reflection pass's texture on the HDR WebGPU path starts at the top row instead. Read it with `reflection_uv`, which turns the rows.

A scene pass draws the scene's background unless a `clearColor` replaces it. A light that only a pass sees casts no shadow there.

A render target the size of the canvas or a share of it takes `scale: 1`, `0.5` or `0.25` in place of `size`. It then follows the render size. A render target that a `ShaderPass` fills becomes a full-screen pass: `render.addPass({ kind: 'fullscreen', wgsl, writes, size or scale, textures })`.

entries.three: renderer.setViewport / setScissor (split screens, picture in picture)
entries.target: scene.createView({ camera, rect }): one scene drawn again from another camera, into a rectangle of the canvas, after the camera's view
entries.notes: `rect` is `[x, y, width, height]` as fractions of the canvas from its top-left corner. Give each view its own camera, and call `setRect` to change the rectangle without allocating. The camera's own view draws the whole canvas first.
entries.details:
A split screen that covers the canvas draws the scene once for the camera and once for each view. Each view costs one cull and one scene draw at its rectangle's pixels. The sun's shadows and the lights cost nothing more.

A view's objects take no ambient occlusion or screen-space reflections. The camera's volumetric fog and outline reach the whole image, a view's rectangle included.

For a minimap that a material shows in the world, a scene pass into a texture (`textures.fromPass`) is cheaper than a view. `destroy` removes the view.

entries.target: engine.capabilities on the page, and ctx.engine.capabilities in the sketch
entries.notes: Reports the GPU tier, limits and features. Never branch on GPU names: some browsers hide them.

entries.target: Nothing to do; createEngine({ largeWorld: true }) and batch origins for planet-scale scenes
entries.notes: The engine draws reversed depth in a 32-bit float buffer. On WebGL2 without `EXT_clip_control`, that depth keeps GL's range, which is less precise. `engine.capabilities.depth` says which depth the device draws.
entries.details: The engine renders relative to the camera through per-cell offsets. With `largeWorld: true`, positions keep their full precision at any distance. `createInstances` also takes an origin that its rows are relative to. The page switch `?depth=standard` draws depth as three.js's `WebGLRenderer` does by default. That helps compare pictures with a three.js original. The switch works on WebGL2 only and draws no shadows.

entries.target: The scene from the sketch context: defineSketch(({ scene }) => ...)
entries.notes: Objects are created in the scene directly.

entries.target: scene.setEnvironment(await assets.loadEnvironment('/env/sunset.ktx2'))
entries.notes: `loadEnvironment` takes an HDR file, or a map from `bunx @null3d/cli assets env` that needs no filtering. `pmremGenerator.fromScene(new RoomEnvironment(), 0.04)` becomes `await assets.builtinEnvironment('room')`, with the same blur and no file. `scene.environmentIntensity` becomes the `intensity` option.
entries.details:
`pmremGenerator.fromScene(sceneWithSky)` becomes `await assets.skyEnvironment()`, called once. Its map follows `scene.setBackground({ sky })`, so drop calls that rebuild the map after each change. The map leaves out the sun's disc, whose light the directional light gives.

The standard material takes the environment's light with three.js's split-sum table, energy compensation and specular occlusion. three.js's PMREM blurs a little less than GGX. So each roughness reads the level that matches three.js's light best.

entries.target: scene.setFog({ curve: 'linear', color, near, far })
entries.notes: The linear curve keeps three.js's smooth step and its defaults of 1 and 1000. null3D measures the straight-line distance from the camera, where three.js measures depth along the view. So fog at the screen's corners is a little thicker, and it no longer shifts as the camera turns.
entries.details:
null3D mixes the fog in linear color before the tone mapping, as `WebGPURenderer` does. It does the same as `WebGLRenderer` when that draws into a half-float target. Only `WebGLRenderer`'s default 8-bit canvas mixes the fog after the sRGB encoding. There the same fog looks a little darker at middle distances.

Materials opt out with `fog: false`. For new scenes, the default exponential curve looks more like real haze. The fog can also thin with height (`heightFalloff`) and glow toward the sun (`sunGlow`).

entries.target: scene.setFog({ curve: 'exp2', color, density })
entries.notes: Pass three.js's density; its default there is 0.00025, and null3D's is 0.01. null3D measures the straight-line distance from the camera, where three.js measures depth along the view. So fog at the screen's corners is a little thicker, and it no longer shifts as the camera turns.
entries.details: null3D mixes the fog in linear color before the tone mapping, as `WebGPURenderer` does. It does the same as `WebGLRenderer` when that draws into a half-float target. Only `WebGLRenderer`'s default 8-bit canvas mixes the fog after the sRGB encoding. There the same fog looks a little darker at middle distances. Materials opt out with `fog: false`.

entries.target: scene.setFog({ color, density, heightFalloff, volumetric: { intensity, anisotropy, distance } })
entries.notes: three.js has no lit fog in core. Its webgpu_volume_lighting example marches rays through a box, lit by point and spot lights with shadows. null3D lights the scene's own fog instead, in a grid that follows the camera's view, with the sun's cascades and the lights' shadows.
entries.details:
Drop the box. The fog's `density` and `heightFalloff` say where the air holds haze, and its scattering intensity becomes `intensity`. The god ray effects of add-on libraries blur a mask of the sky toward the sun on the screen. null3D's rays also come from lamps and from shadows off the screen.

The rays draw where the quality setting `fogSlices` is above 0: Medium and up. On Low the fog keeps its `sunGlow`.

entries.target: scene.createGroup({ name, position })
child.setParent(parent); setParent(parent, { keepWorld: true }) for attach(); getParent() for object.parent; destroy() to remove
entries.notes: Objects are in the scene as soon as they are created. `setParent` keeps the local transform, like `add()`, and `getParent()` returns the parent, or null for a root object. Creating, destroying and re-parenting rebuild the draw tables in that frame, so hide with `setVisible` and pool with `setActiveCount` during play (guides/performance).
entries.details: Under a parent turned and scaled by different amounts per axis, `keepWorld` keeps the child in place. Its rotation and scale then come out close to the old ones, as with `attach()`.

entries.target: obj.setPosition(x, y, z); obj.translate(x, y, z) for translateX/Y/Z
entries.notes: translate moves along the object's own axes, as translateX, translateY and translateZ do together. For many moving objects, use an instance batch and write its positions array directly instead of calling setters.

entries.target: obj.setRotationEuler(x, y, z, 'XYZ'), obj.rotateX/Y/Z(angle), or obj.setRotation(qx, qy, qz, qw)
entries.notes: Euler order strings match three.js. rotateX, rotateY and rotateZ turn the object about its own axes, as in three.js. For rotateOnAxis, multiply the quaternion from obj.getRotation by one from quat.setAxisAngle, and pass the product to setRotation.

entries.target: obj.setRotation(x, y, z, w), with the quaternion from quat.setAxisAngle, quat.fromEuler, quat.multiply or quat.slerp
entries.notes: The quat helpers write into an array that you create once with quat.create(). Pass its four numbers to setRotation. The rotations array of an instance batch takes the same order.

entries.target: obj.setScale(x, y, z)
obj.lookAt(x, y, z)
entries.notes: Meshes and groups turn their +Z axis to the point. Cameras and lights turn their -Z axis there, as in three.js. The call assumes that the object's parents are not rotated.

entries.target: obj.getWorldPosition(out), obj.getWorldQuaternion(out), obj.getWorldMatrix(out)
entries.notes: Each getter copies into an array that you make once, with vec3.create(), quat.create() or mat4.create(). They read the engine's last transform update, so a change made in onUpdate shows in the same frame's onLateUpdate. getWorldMatrix gives 16 numbers, column by column, like matrixWorld.elements.

entries.target: Nothing to do: objects are static by default and update when a setter changes them; create objects that move every frame with dynamic: true
entries.notes: Remove manual matrix calls. Move single objects with their setters. Only instance batches take writes to their typed arrays, and a static batch uploads only the rows you mark with markDirty.

entries.target: scene.find(name) for getObjectByName; scene.listObjects() at setup, or your own arrays of objects, instead of traverse and children
entries.notes: `scene.find(name)` returns the first object created with that name, from an index. `scene.listObjects()` returns every object as a new array, and `getParent()` returns an object's parent. No call returns an object's children, so keep the objects you need in arrays.
entries.details: `scene.listObjects` walks the whole scene and allocates. Call it at setup, never in every frame.

entries.target: obj.setVisible(false)
entries.notes: Hiding is cheap: it uploads the object's matrix and draw entry. It never rebuilds the draw tables, so use it instead of removing and adding objects during play. The objects under a hidden object, dynamic ones too, stop updating until it shows again.
entries.details: three.js updates the matrices of hidden objects anyway. So hide a pool of spare objects under one parent.

entries.target: mesh.setCastShadows(true) / setReceiveShadows(true), or the castShadows and receiveShadows options of createMesh
entries.notes: Both flags are false by default, as in three.js. The directional, spot and point lights cast them on both GPU paths. Point lights cast where the preset's `pointLightShadows` is on.
entries.details: Unlit materials show no shadows. An instance batch takes `castShadows` and `receiveShadows` in `createInstances`. `batch.setCastShadows(true)` and `setReceiveShadows(true)` set them for every row.

entries.target: obj.setLayers(mask), obj.getLayers(), camera.setLayers(mask), batch.setLayers(mask); the layers option of createMesh, createInstances and createPerspectiveCamera
entries.notes: Masks use the same 32 bits and the same default of layer 0 alone. A camera draws an object when their masks share a bit. `layers.set(n)` becomes `setLayers(1 << n)`, and `enableAll()` becomes `setLayers(0xffffffff)`.
entries.details:
For enable and disable, read the mask with `getLayers()` and pass the new mask. `layers.mask` becomes `getLayers()`. An `InstancedMesh`'s layers become its batch's, for every row. Raycasts and declared passes take layer masks.

Shadow casters differ. three.js tests them against the camera's layers, and null3D tests them against the light's. Give each shadow-casting light the layers of every object that must cast. Otherwise those objects cast nothing.

entries.target: mesh.setRenderOrder(n)
entries.notes: Lower orders draw first, before their depth, as in three.js. An object's depth is the depth of its bounding sphere's center, as in three.js. The engine orders opaque and masked objects itself for speed.
entries.details: The rows of an instance batch sort by depth one by one. three.js sorts an `InstancedMesh` as one object.

entries.target: mesh.setFrustumCulled(false)
entries.notes: Usually needed only for shader-displaced geometry; prefer mesh.setBounds(center, radius) with larger bounds, which keeps culling at work.

entries.target: Your own arrays, or a Map keyed by the object
entries.notes: Engine objects have no userData, and their TypeScript types refuse new properties. A Map from each object to its data keeps the data beside the object. Arrays indexed the way your sketch counts objects stay fastest in per-frame loops.

entries.target: onUpdate / onLateUpdate, or a declared pass
entries.notes: The engine draws from lists that the sketch records, so it calls no sketch code per draw. Move per-object work into onUpdate or onLateUpdate.

entries.target: scene.instantiate(prefab) for loaded models; scene.clone(obj) for built objects
entries.notes: Each instantiate shares the model's meshes, materials and textures. scene.clone copies an object and every object below it, lights and cameras included, under the same parent. A copy of an animated model gets an animator of its own, as SkeletonUtils.clone gives a copy its own skeleton.

entries.target: texture.destroy(); material.destroy(); mesh.destroy(); prefab.destroy() for a loaded glTF model
entries.notes: `texture.destroy()` frees a texture's GPU memory, and `material.destroy()` frees the material's place. `mesh.destroy()` frees a mesh's GPU memory at the next frame, and throws E1111 while an object or batch uses it. Destroy objects and batches first, then the mesh.
entries.details:
Objects that still use a destroyed material draw nothing. A custom material's pipelines free with its last material. `prefab.destroy()` frees every mesh, material and texture of a loaded model, and its skeleton and clips. It waits until its copies are destroyed.

three.js's `dispose` leaves the object usable and uploads it again on the next render. null3D's destroy ends it, and later calls throw E1101.

entries.target: scene.overrideMaterial = material, and null for each object's own material
entries.notes: The material draws every mesh and instance batch of the main pass. Each keeps its mesh, place and instances, as three.js does. Sprites, points, lines and particle systems keep their own materials, and the shadow maps keep each object's material.
entries.details: A masked caster still cuts its shadow. A sprite, point or line material throws E1224. The change rebuilds the draw tables in the next frame, and adds no draw call or pipeline after that.

entries.target: scene.setEnvironment(env, { rotation }) and scene.setBackground(env, { rotation })
entries.notes: Rotation is an Euler array in radians, in the order X, Y, Z, as in three.js. Each material shares the scene's rotation, so material.envMapRotation has none of its own. scene.setBackground turns environments and cube maps, not textures or the sky.

entries.target: scene.setBackground(env, { blur, intensity })
entries.notes: Each `setBackground` call sets that background's options, where three.js keeps them on the scene. The blur reads the environment's level for that roughness, so it costs nothing extra. Only environments blur: ask `assets.loadEnvironment` for one.
entries.details: three.js turns a blurred `CubeTexture` into a PMREM texture. `intensity` applies to textures, environments, cube maps and the sky.

entries.target: scene.createPerspectiveCamera({ fov, near, far, position, target })
entries.notes: `fov` is vertical and in degrees, as in three.js, and the aspect ratio is automatic. The `fov`, `near` and `far` properties are read-only: change them with `camera.setFov` and `camera.setNearFar`. The defaults are three.js's: fov 50, near 0.1 and far 2000.

entries.target: camera.setFocalLength(mm) and camera.focalLength
entries.notes: null3D's sensor is full frame, 24 mm tall along the canvas's height, so a focal length gives the same view on every canvas shape. three.js measures its 35 mm `filmGauge` along the longer side. The two agree on a square canvas with `filmGauge` 24.
entries.details: Depth of field takes the camera's focal length unless its settings give one.

entries.three: OrthographicCamera(left, right, top, bottom, near, far)
entries.target: scene.createOrthographicCamera({ height, near, far, position, target }), or left, right, top and bottom in place of height
entries.notes: With `height` alone, the width follows the canvas's aspect ratio, so resize code goes away. The four edges keep their shape on any canvas, as in three.js. To zoom, call `camera.setOrthoHeight` with the original height divided by three.js's zoom.
entries.details: The default height of 2 gives the same view as three.js's default edges, -1 to 1.

entries.three: camera.setViewOffset(fullWidth, fullHeight, x, y, width, height) / clearViewOffset()
entries.target: camera.setLensShift(x, y) and camera.lensShift, on perspective and orthographic cameras
entries.notes: A lens shift moves the view off the camera's axis and keeps the perspective. It counts in fractions of the view's width and height, with y up. A full-size view offset becomes `setLensShift(x / fullWidth, -y / fullHeight)`, and `clearViewOffset()` becomes `setLensShift(0, 0)`.
entries.details:
For an offset that draws one tile of a larger picture, also narrow the lens on a canvas of the tile's shape. Set the half angle's tangent to `tan(fov / 2) * height / fullHeight`. An orthographic camera's height becomes `height / fullHeight` of the full one. Then shift by `((x + width / 2) / fullWidth - 0.5) * fullWidth / width` across. Shift by `(0.5 - (y + height / 2) / fullHeight) * fullHeight / height` up.

Culling, shadows, picking, `screenToRay`, `worldToScreen`, labels and views all follow the shift. Delete code that turns the camera to move a subject off center. A turn makes upright lines lean.

entries.target: camera.worldToScreen(point, out) for [x, y, depth]; camera.screenToRay(x, y, ray) for a ray through a point
entries.notes: Both take and give CSS pixels from the canvas's top-left corner, not device coordinates. The depth is the distance in front of the camera, and below 0 behind it. A ray through the pointer uses the camera of the frame on screen at the event.
entries.details: three.js starts an orthographic ray on the camera's plane. `screenToRay` starts it on the near plane.

entries.target: scene.createReflectionProbe({ box: { min, max }, position, refresh: 'always' }); a reflection pass for a flat mirror: render.addPass({ kind: 'reflection', writes, plane })
entries.notes: A `CubeCamera` with a `WebGLCubeRenderTarget`, filtered by `PMREMGenerator`, becomes a reflection probe. The probe captures the scene from its position on the GPU and filters it for each roughness. `cubeCamera.update()` in every frame becomes `refresh: 'always'`, and one update after a change becomes `probe.capture()`.
entries.details:
The probe lights every surface inside its box, not one material. Its box projects the reflections, so walls reflect at their own distance. Give the probe a box around the space that the object moves in. `boxProjection: false` reads it as three.js reads a cube map, as light from far away.

The near and far of the `CubeCamera` fall away. Captures draw from 5 cm out to the camera's far plane. Leave the reflecting object out of its own probe's captures with layers.

entries.target: None; split screens use scene.createView with one camera for each view
entries.notes: null3D has no stereo rendering. For split screens, give each view a camera and a rectangle of the canvas.

entries.target: scene.createDirectionalLight({ direction, color, intensity, castShadows, shadow })
entries.notes: The light is an object. Pass the target minus the position as `direction`, or call `light.lookAt(x, y, z)` again whenever the target moves. Surfaces show up to four directional lights: the first created casts shadows, and up to three more add fill and rim light.
entries.details:
Delete `shadow.camera` bounds. The engine's shadow cascades fit the view, and the shadow distance follows the farthest visible receiver by default. A port with its own `shadow.camera.far` passes that number as `shadow: { distance }`. The engine also draws contact shadows, which three.js lacks: on High and Ultra, and on Medium on WebGL2. Set `shadow: { contactDistance: 0 }` to match three.js's look.

`intensity` stays in lux, three.js's unit. three.js has no hero shadow. A port that fits a second shadowed light, or a shadow camera, to one object uses `light.setShadow({ hero: object })`, which follows it.

entries.target: scene.createPointLight({ position, color, intensity, range, decay, castShadows, shadow, intensityUnit })
entries.notes: `distance` becomes `range`, which every point light needs; 0 is refused. `intensity` stays in candela, and `light.power` in lumens becomes `intensity` with `intensityUnit: 'lumen'`. `castShadow` becomes `castShadows`; `shadow` takes `bias` and `normalBias` in meters, and `shadow.camera` has no equivalent.
entries.details: `intensityUnit: 'lumen'` divides by 4π as `power` does, and `setIntensity` then takes lumens. The quality preset sets the tile size in place of `shadow.mapSize`.

entries.three: SpotLight(color, intensity, distance, angle, penumbra, decay)
entries.target: scene.createSpotLight({ position, direction | target, angle, penumbra, range, decay, intensity, map, castShadows, shadow, intensityUnit })
entries.notes: `distance` becomes `range`, which every spot light needs, and `intensity` stays in candela. `light.power` in lumens becomes `intensity` with `intensityUnit: 'lumen'`, and `target` is a point. `shadow.camera` has no equivalent: call `light.lookAt(x, y, z)` when the target moves.
entries.details:
`intensityUnit: 'lumen'` divides by π at any cone angle, as `power` does. `castShadow` becomes `castShadows`, and `shadow` takes `bias` and `normalBias` in meters. The quality preset sets the tile size in place of `shadow.mapSize`.

`light.map` becomes `map`: sRGB pixels as `{ width, height, data }`, or an engine texture. `setMap` takes the same. The light projects it over its cone as three.js projects it. Its top row follows the world's up, as three.js aims its map's camera. So a light rolled about its axis shows the same map.

The engine copies a texture into its own light image once. A texture that changes every frame, a `VideoTexture` included, throws E1112. The engine keeps the picture's detail up to 512 texels a side, and reduces a larger texture to that. three.js samples the texture itself. Up to 32 lights show a map at once.

entries.target: scene.createHemisphereLight({ skyColor, groundColor, intensity })
entries.notes: The sky lies along the light's +Y axis: turn the light to tilt it, where three.js moves it. It lights surfaces as three.js's does, diffuse only, and its light adds to the environment's. Any number of them cost the same per pixel.
entries.details: `intensity` stays in lux, three.js's unit.

entries.target: scene.createAmbientLight({ color, intensity })
entries.notes: Several ambient lights add up. intensity stays in lux, three.js's unit.

entries.target: scene.createRectAreaLight({ color, intensity, width, height, range })
entries.notes: It needs a `range`, where three.js's light has no end. The light leaves along -Z, as in three.js, and casts no shadows. The engine shades it with linearly transformed cosines, as three.js does.
entries.details: Delete `RectAreaLightUniformsLib.init()`. `intensity` stays in nits, three.js's unit.

entries.target: Nothing: the engine loads the area lights' tables with the first area light
entries.notes: Remove the init() call.

entries.target: scene.setLightProbeGrid: a grid of irradiance probes lights the scene where a surface stands
entries.notes: One `LightProbe` that lights the whole scene is an environment: `scene.setEnvironment` takes its diffuse spherical harmonics with the environment map. `bunx @null3d/cli assets env` computes that map offline. For light that changes from place to place, bake a grid with `bakeProbes` and set it with `scene.setLightProbeGrid`.
entries.details: The grid holds L1 spherical harmonics per probe, where three.js's `LightProbeGrid` holds L2. The scene page's light probe grid section shows both calls.

entries.three: LightProbeGrid (addons: a baked grid of L2 irradiance probes)
entries.target: scene.setLightProbeGrid with a grid that bakeProbes bakes in the sketch
entries.notes: three.js's grid stores L2 spherical harmonics per probe, and null3D's stores L1. That takes four texture reads per pixel in place of seven: three of coefficients and one of its masks. The light keeps its direction, but small bright patches spread a little wider.
entries.details: three.js adds the grid's light to the environment's diffuse light. null3D's grid takes the environment's place, and the live environment's light times each probe's sky visibility. Bake the grid again with `bakeProbes` when the scene changes.

entries.target: Built in: scene.createPointLight and scene.createSpotLight; the engine clusters every light
entries.notes: Delete the add-on and its setup. null3D sorts point and spot lights into clusters on both GPU paths, and they may cast shadows. three.js's add-on takes point lights without shadows, on WebGPU only.

entries.target: Built in: shadow: { cascades } on the directional light
entries.notes: Delete the addon: its `cascades`, `maxFar` and `shadowMapSize` become the `cascades`, `distance` and `mapSize` settings. The cascades keep still edges as the camera turns, and far cascades draw every few frames. The `mode` setting has no equivalent.
entries.details:
The `farCascadeInterval` quality setting says how often far cascades draw. The `fade` option is on by default: neighboring cascades blend over a band, which the `shadowCascadeBlend` quality setting sizes. `fade: false` maps to `shadowCascadeBlend: 0`.

The `mode` setting has no equivalent. The engine's split leans a little more toward the camera than the addon's practical mode, so its near cascade is shorter. `debug.shadowCamera(camera)` lets the cascades follow a camera other than the one that renders, as the addon's `camera` option does. It works in development builds only.

entries.target: scene.createDirectionalLight({ direction, castShadows: true, shadow: { cascades: 2 } })
entries.notes: Delete the add-on. The directional light's shadow takes cascades fitted to the camera's view, with a blend between neighbors. SunLight's two cascades become `cascades: 2`.
entries.details: The CSM entry maps the other settings.

entries.target: Contact shadows of the directional light: scene.createDirectionalLight({ castShadows: true, shadow: { contactDistance } })
entries.notes: Both search the camera's depth toward the main light for short shadows where objects touch. `shadow.contactDistance` sets their reach in meters, 0.3 by default. Only the first directional light draws them, while it casts shadows.
entries.details: They draw where the quality setting `contactShadowSteps` is above 0: on High and Ultra, and on Medium on WebGL2.

entries.three: light.shadow.mapSize / bias / normalBias / intensity / radius / camera
entries.target: shadow: { mapSize, bias, normalBias, intensity, cascades, distance } in the directional light's options, or light.setShadow()
entries.notes: `mapSize` is one number, the texels on each side. `bias` and `normalBias` are in meters, where three.js gives `bias` in depth units, so start from the defaults. `shadow.camera` has no equivalent, and `shadowSide` has no option.
entries.details:
`intensity` is 0 to 1 and carries over as it stands. The directional light's map stores 16-bit depth. In each cascade, `bias` covers at least 1.5 of its depth steps. That is about 2 cm in a far cascade 200 m out.

`radius` and `blurSamples` become the `shadowFilter` quality setting, 3 or 5 texels on each side. `shadow.camera` has no equivalent: the cascades fit the camera's view. The shader mixes each shadow lookup toward full light by the rest, at no cost to the frame.

Casters draw only the faces that point away from the light, as three.js's default `shadowSide` does. Double-sided materials draw both.

entries.target: Physical light units, as in three.js r155 and later
entries.notes: Scenes tuned in three.js's legacy light mode need new intensities: retune them with parity images.

entries.three: Box / Sphere / Plane / Cylinder / Cone / Torus / Capsule / Circle / Ring Geometry
entries.target: geometry.box({ width, height, depth }), geometry.sphere({ radius }), and one generator for each class
entries.notes: Constructor arguments become options with the same names and defaults. `new CylinderGeometry(0.3, 0.4, 2)` is `geometry.cylinder({ radiusTop: 0.3, radiusBottom: 0.4, height: 2 })`. The meshes match three.js's vertices, normals, texture coordinates and triangles.
entries.details: Each object has one material. An array of materials for the face groups of a box or a cylinder needs one object for each group.

entries.three: geometry.rotateX / rotateY / rotateZ / translate / scale / center / applyMatrix4
entries.target: obj.setRotationEuler(x, y, z), obj.setPosition(x, y, z) or obj.setScale(x, y, z) on the object that draws the mesh
entries.notes: A mesh keeps the vertices its generator built, so the transform goes on the object or instance row. `floor.setRotationEuler(-Math.PI / 2, 0, 0)` lays a plane flat. To build the transform into the vertices, transform the arrays and pass them to `geometry.fromArrays`.

entries.three: TorusKnot / Icosahedron / Octahedron / Tetrahedron / Dodecahedron / Polyhedron / Lathe / Extrude / Shape / Tube Geometry
entries.target: geometry.fromArrays(torusKnot({ radius, tube, tubularSegments, radialSegments, p, q })), and icosahedron, octahedron, tetrahedron, dodecahedron, polyhedron, lathe, shape, extrude and tube, from @null3d/geometry
entries.notes: Install `@null3d/geometry`. Each function takes the constructor's arguments as named options with three.js's defaults, and returns arrays for `geometry.fromArrays`. `Shape`, `Path`, the curves and `ShapeUtils` keep their names and methods, but points are arrays.
entries.details: `ExtrudeGeometry`'s caps and sides form one mesh, which takes one material. `CurvePath.getPoint(t)`, and `Path`'s and `Shape`'s, throws a `RangeError` when `t` is above 1 or the path is empty. three.js returns null there. A custom `UVGenerator`'s `generateTopUV` and `generateSideWallUV` take no geometry argument first, so drop it. A list of shapes makes one mesh with one material, where `ShapeGeometry` gives each shape a group. Make one shape call per material.

entries.target: geometry.fromArrays({ positions, normals, uvs, uvs1, colors, tangents, joints, weights, indices })
entries.notes: `geometry.fromArrays` returns a mesh that `createMesh` and `createInstances` accept. The attributes `position`, `normal`, `uv`, `uv1`, `color` and `tangent` each become one array, and `setIndex` becomes `indices`, 16-bit or 32-bit. The engine copies the arrays.
entries.details: `skinIndex` and `skinWeight` become `joints` and `weights`. 8-bit and 16-bit integer arrays stay integers on the GPU. `{ array, normalized: true }` keeps a `BufferAttribute`'s normalized flag.

entries.three: attribute.needsUpdate / setUsage(DynamicDrawUsage) / addUpdateRange (vertices changing every frame)
entries.target: mesh.updateVertices(name, values, start, count)
entries.notes: Pass the attribute's values of every vertex, in the array type the mesh was made with. `start` and `count` pick the vertices that change, as `addUpdateRange` does, but in vertices. The mesh keeps the bounding sphere it was made with, so call `setBounds` when vertices move outside it.
entries.details: Meshes with joints or morph targets take no updates. For many moving objects, use instances instead of rewriting vertices.

entries.target: geometry.fromArrays({ ..., computeNormals: true, computeTangents: true })
entries.notes: The results match three.js's bit for bit. computeTangents needs uvs, and works without indices too. Bounds are always automatic, so computeBoundingSphere and computeBoundingBox need no call.

entries.target: WireframeGeometry: a material with wireframe: true on the mesh itself. EdgesGeometry: scene.createLines({ positions, mode: 'segments' }) with two points per edge
entries.notes: A wireframe material draws each triangle's three edges, as WireframeGeometry lists them, with no copy of the mesh. null3D does not find a mesh's feature edges for you, as EdgesGeometry does with its angle threshold. Build that list of edge points from the mesh's arrays, or with EdgesGeometry at build time, and draw it as pairs of points.

entries.target: DOM labels (ui.trackLabel), a texture with pre-rendered text, or a text mesh baked into glTF
entries.notes: null3D draws no text of its own. Use DOM labels for text that follows an object, a texture for text on a surface, and a baked mesh for 3D letters.

entries.target: mesh.setMorphWeight(indexOrName, weight) and mesh.getMorphWeight(indexOrName); geometry.fromArrays({ ..., morphTargets: { positions, normals, colors, names } })
entries.notes: glTF morph targets and their default weights load with the model, and its clips animate the weights. Targets are deltas, as with `morphTargetsRelative = true`. `mesh.mesh.morphTargetNames` lists the names in target order, in place of `morphTargetDictionary`.
entries.details:
Color targets (`morphAttributes.color`, glTF's COLOR_0 targets) change vertex colors, so the mesh needs colors too. The colors stay between 0 and 1 as glTF asks; three.js does not clamp them. A glTF target without COLOR_0, while another target has it, changes no color, as glTF says. three.js r186 adds the base color there.

Tangent targets morph tangents, as glTF gives them, which three.js does not do. A clip blends its weights with the object's own, as `AnimationMixer` does. On WebGL2 each object draws only its largest weights, by the `morphTargets` quality setting: 8 on Low up to 64 on Ultra.

entries.target: materials.standard({ color, map, metalness, roughness, normalMap, aoMap, emissive, ... })
entries.notes: Both follow glTF's metallic-roughness model with the same formulas, so color, metalness, roughness and emissive carry over. `roughnessMap` and `metalnessMap` become one `metalnessRoughnessMap`. A texture's repeat, offset and rotation become the material's `uvTransform`, or a per-map `mapUvTransforms` entry.
entries.details: Roughness has three.js r187's floor of 0.045. Highlights on small curved shapes widen by Filament's specular anti-aliasing. three.js adds its own term, so they are a little brighter and narrower there. A normal map that tilts a reflection below the surface fades the environment's reflection, which three.js does not. A normal map on a mesh without tangents takes its frame from how positions and texture coordinates change between pixels, as in three.js.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial (clearcoat, transmission, dispersion, sheen, iridescence, anisotropy, specular)
entries.target: materials.standard, with ior, specularIntensity, specularColor and their maps, transmission, dispersion, clearcoat, sheen, iridescence and anisotropy
entries.notes: `materials.standard` takes `ior`, `specularIntensity`, `specularColor` and their maps, `transmission`, `dispersion`, `clearcoat`, `sheen`, `iridescence` and `anisotropy`. Each uses three.js's names and formulas, with the detail on its own entry.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial ior / reflectivity / specularIntensity / specularColor / specularIntensityMap / specularColorMap
entries.target: materials.standard({ ior, specularIntensity, specularColor, specularIntensityMap, specularColorMap })
entries.notes: Same names, ranges and formulas, so the values carry over, and glTF's `KHR_materials_ior` and `KHR_materials_specular` load into them. `specularColor` takes linear components above 1, as three.js's Color does. `reflectivity` has no option: set `ior = (1 + 0.4 * reflectivity) / (1 - 0.4 * reflectivity)`, as three.js converts it.
entries.details: A glTF `ior` of 0 becomes 1000, as `GLTFLoader` reads it.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial transmission / thickness / attenuationColor / attenuationDistance / dispersion
entries.target: materials.standard({ transmission, thickness, ior, dispersion, roughness, attenuationColor, attenuationDistance })
entries.notes: Same names, ranges and formulas, and glTF's transmission, volume and dispersion extensions load into them. Give `transmission` when you create the material, even as 0, to change it later. A masked material keeps its transmission, and the hash alpha mode has no counterpart and throws.
entries.details:
The surface samples a mipmapped copy of the opaque objects' colors where its bent ray leaves the volume, as three.js does. The copy holds opaque objects only. three.js also draws the back faces of double-sided glass into it. Where the bent ray lands on an opaque object in front of the surface, null3D shows what lies straight behind. three.js shows that object's color.

`transmissionMap` and `thicknessMap` keep row slots of their own and sample the specular slots' arrays. The red and green channels there scale the transmission and the thickness. So a material with them may also give the specular maps where the two textures share an array.

A thickness map never shares a specular color map's array, because one is linear and the other sRGB. A development build refuses that pair. A layered material keeps the two maps beside its layers, unless a layer map fills the array that one of them samples. A development build refuses that too.

`dispersion` spreads the index of refraction over three rays, one per color, with red taking the lowest. A prism then separates the light behind it into colors. Its cost falls on the materials that set it. A custom material sets `s.transmission` in its surface function.

entries.three: MeshSSSNodeMaterial / SubsurfaceScatteringShader (thicknessColor, thicknessDistortion, thicknessAmbient, thicknessAttenuation, thicknessPower, thicknessScale, thicknessMap)
entries.target: materials.standard({ diffuseTransmission, diffuseTransmissionColor, diffuseTransmissionMap, doubleSided: true }), with subsurfaceRadius and subsurfaceColor for skin
entries.notes: Light from behind a thin surface shows on its front through glTF's diffuse transmission, which `KHR_materials_diffuse_transmission` also loads. Map `thicknessColor`, `thicknessScale` and `thicknessMap` to the diffuse transmission options. `thicknessDistortion` and `thicknessPower` have no option, and the front keeps `1 - diffuseTransmission` of its light.
entries.details:
`thicknessScale` stays between 0 and 1, and the thickness map's value sits in alpha. `thicknessAmbient` maps to the ambient and environment light, which shine through by themselves.

three.js's term glows most when the camera looks toward the light. `thicknessDistortion` and `thicknessPower` shape the glow. null3D's light from behind spreads evenly, as glTF describes. So those two have no option, and the glow looks softer head on.

For skin, wax and marble, add `subsurfaceRadius` and `subsurfaceColor`. The subsurface blur spreads the diffuse light on the High and Ultra presets. A custom material sets `s.diffuseTransmission` in its surface function.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial clearcoat / clearcoatRoughness / clearcoatNormalScale / clearcoatMap / clearcoatRoughnessMap / clearcoatNormalMap
entries.target: materials.standard({ clearcoat, clearcoatRoughness, clearcoatNormalScale, clearcoatMap, clearcoatRoughnessMap, clearcoatNormalMap })
entries.notes: Same names, ranges and formulas, and glTF's `KHR_materials_clearcoat` loads into them. Give a clear coat option when you create the material, even as 0, to change it later. `clearcoatMap` and `clearcoatRoughnessMap` must be one texture, with the coat in red and its roughness in green.
entries.details:
Pack two textures into one for that pair. A material with a clear coat or a sheen takes no `lightMap`, `specularIntensityMap` or `specularColorMap`. A custom material sets `s.clearcoat` in its surface function.

The car paint example add-on (guides/car-paint) builds metal flakes and panel seams over this clear coat. three.js has no flake lobe: its metal flakes are a normal map.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial iridescence / iridescenceIOR / iridescenceThicknessRange / iridescenceMap / iridescenceThicknessMap
entries.target: materials.standard({ iridescence, iridescenceIor, iridescenceThicknessRange, iridescenceMap, iridescenceThicknessMap })
entries.notes: The same thin-film formulas apply, and glTF's `KHR_materials_iridescence` loads into them. three.js names the index of refraction `iridescenceIOR` and takes its thickness as one range. Give `iridescenceIor` and `iridescenceThicknessRange`, in nanometers.
entries.details: Give an iridescence option when you create the material to change it later. A material with iridescence takes no `lightMap`, `specularIntensityMap` or `specularColorMap`, and no clear coat's or sheen's maps. A custom material sets `s.iridescence`, `s.iridescenceIor` and `s.iridescenceThickness` in its surface function.

entries.target: materials.standard({ anisotropy, anisotropyRotation, anisotropyMap })
entries.notes: The same anisotropic GGX lobe applies, with three.js's formulas, and glTF's `KHR_materials_anisotropy` loads into it. Leave the map out and the stretch still draws: its direction comes from the mesh's tangents, else the texture coordinates. A surface with neither takes a steady direction of its own.
entries.details: It takes no `lightMap`, `specularIntensityMap` or `specularColorMap`, and no clear coat's or sheen's maps. Rectangles and tubes of light shade it as three.js does, without the stretch.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial sheen / sheenColor / sheenRoughness / sheenColorMap / sheenRoughnessMap
entries.target: materials.standard({ sheenColor, sheenRoughness, sheenColorMap, sheenRoughnessMap })
entries.notes: The same Charlie sheen applies, with three.js's formulas, and glTF's `KHR_materials_sheen` loads into it. There is no `sheen` option: give `sheenColor` times three.js's `sheen`, which defaults to 0. Give a sheen option when you create the material to change it later.
entries.details: A three.js material without sheen shows none, so its port leaves the sheen options out. `sheenColorMap` and `sheenRoughnessMap` must be one texture, with the roughness in alpha, as glTF packs them. A material with a clear coat or a sheen takes no `lightMap`, `specularIntensityMap` or `specularColorMap`.

entries.three: DecalGeometry (addon), with a material that has polygonOffset
entries.target: scene.createMesh({ mesh: geometry.box(), material: materials.decal({ map, normalMap, roughness }), position, rotation, scale: size })
entries.notes: No geometry is cut: the box projects the material onto every opaque surface inside it. It draws in a pass after the opaque objects, lit by every light and shadow. `DecalGeometry`'s position, orientation and size become the box's position, rotation and scale.
entries.details:
The image lies on the box's x and y sides and looks along its z axis, as `DecalGeometry` lays it. There is no target mesh: the decal marks every opaque surface in its box. `polygonOffset`, `depthWrite: false` and `transparent: true` are not needed.

`angleFade` and `edgeFade` fade the decal on surfaces that turn away and near the box's ends, where `DecalGeometry` stretches the image. A batch of boxes with one decal material draws many decals in one draw. Blended surfaces show no decals. Projected texture libraries, such as three-projected-material, become a large decal box.

entries.target: materials.unlit({ color, map, opacity, alphaMode, vertexColors })
entries.notes: Its map's alpha and the vertex alpha join the opacity, as in three.js. The exposure and the tone mapping apply to it, as three.js applies them.

entries.target: materials.standard with metalness 0 and roughness near 1 (Lambert), or roughness tuned to the Phong shininess
entries.notes: Expect small visual differences: the standard material adds a faint highlight and keeps energy as three.js's MeshStandardMaterial does. Compare screenshots of both versions, then accept or tune.

entries.target: materials.shader({ wgsl, uniforms }) with a toon surface function
entries.notes: A surface function cannot read the scene's lights. Pass the light direction as a uniform, step the light into bands, and return the result as emissive. A lobe function, `fn lobe(input: LobeInput) -> vec3f`, does read each light.
entries.details:
The engine calls the lobe for the main directional light and for each point and spot light, with the light's direction and its shadowed irradiance. It adds the lobe's color to that light's specular, beside the base lighting. So bands made there follow every such light and its shadows.

Set the surface's `baseColor` to black and its roughness to 1, as the uniform recipe does, so the base lighting adds little beside the bands. The engine calls no lobe for the fill directional lights and the area lights. So the bands do not follow them.

entries.target: debug.view('normals' | 'depth') for debugging; matcap is a recipe with an unlit function, fn unlit
entries.notes: debug.view shades the whole scene, in development builds only. Its normals are in world space, where MeshNormalMaterial's are in view space. Its depth is white at the near plane, on a logarithmic scale for a perspective camera.

entries.target: materials.shader({ wgsl, uniforms, textures }) with a WGSL surface function, an unlit function (fn unlit), or a full WGSL shader
entries.notes: Rewrite in WGSL, in one literal tagged `/* wgsl */`. Prefer a surface function, so lighting, shadows, fog and instancing keep working. A shader that ignores the lights becomes an unlit function, `fn unlit`, which keeps the uniforms, the textures and the fog.
entries.details:
The built-ins that `ShaderMaterial` adds have WGSL names of their own (see the ShaderMaterial built-ins entry). Declare the uniforms once, as `struct Uniforms`. Updates such as `material.uniforms.uSpeed.value = 2` become `material.set({ speed: 2 })`. The type check rejects a name that `struct Uniforms` lacks.

A `sampler2D` uniform becomes `var name: texture_2d<f32>;` in the WGSL and an entry of the `textures` option. Sample it with `textureSample(name, nameSampler, uv)`. Textures are fixed when the material is created. Full shaders take no textures.

entries.target: materials.shader({ wgsl }) with a surface function or a vertex-offset function
entries.notes: The engine has no shader chunks to patch. Keep the standard options on the new material: defaultSurface applies them. A custom material takes no standard maps (map, normalMap and the rest): declare textures in the WGSL and pass them with the textures option.

entries.three: A ShaderMaterial that samples the scene's depth texture
entries.target: materials.shader({ sceneInputs: ['sceneDepth'], wgsl }) with sceneDepth(uv) or sceneDistance(uv)
entries.notes: Declare `sceneInputs: ['sceneDepth']` and read the opaque scene's depth in the surface function, with `uv = input.fragCoord.xy / frame.resolution`. The engine binds a copy of the opaque depth. `sceneDepth` gives 1 at the near plane and 0 at the far plane, and `sceneDistance` gives the distance in world units.
entries.details: A surface in the opaque pass, or in a scene or reflection pass, reads 0, the far plane.

entries.three: ShaderMaterial built-ins: uv1, gl_FragCoord, gl_InstanceID / instanceIndex, modelMatrix, normalMatrix, viewMatrix, projectionMatrix, cameraNear, cameraFar
entries.target: input.uv1, input.fragCoord, input.instance, object.worldMatrix, object.normalMatrix, camera.view, camera.projection, camera.near, camera.far
entries.notes: The engine works relative to the camera, so its matrices do too. `object.worldMatrix` has its translation relative to the camera, and `camera.view` holds the camera's rotation only. `camera.projection * camera.view * object.worldMatrix` places a vertex, as `projectionMatrix * modelViewMatrix` does.
entries.details:
`object.position` gives the origin in the world. `object.normalMatrix` turns normals into world space, where three.js's `normalMatrix` turns them into view space. Multiply by `camera.view` for view space. `camera.projection` has reversed depth, 1 at the near plane. `input.fragCoord` counts from the top left, so `gl_FragCoord.y` becomes `frame.resolution.y - input.fragCoord.y`.

`input.instance` is the row in an instance batch, 0 for an object of the scene. `object.id` and `mesh.shaderId` tell objects apart, which three.js leaves to uniforms. Only WGSL that reads `uv1`, `instance`, an id or the object's matrices pays for them.

entries.target: materials.shader({ wgsl }) with a WGSL surface function
entries.notes: Most TSL nodes map to one WGSL expression; see the shader porting reference.

entries.three: transparent / opacity / alphaTest / depthWrite / depthTest / blending / vertexColors / flatShading / colorWrite
entries.target: alphaMode: 'blend' | 'mask' (with alphaCutoff), depthWrite, depthTest, colorWrite, blending: 'normal' | 'additive' | 'multiply' | 'weighted', vertexColors, flatShading
entries.notes: `transparent: true` becomes `alphaMode: 'blend'`, and `alphaTest` becomes `alphaMode: 'mask'` with `alphaCutoff`. `depthTest: false` writes no depth either, as in three.js's WebGL renderer. `colorWrite: false` writes depth and no color.
entries.details:
Its objects draw before the opaque objects that write color, so the depth holds back their color behind the surface. three.js orders that by material. `blending` takes effect with `alphaMode: 'blend'` only. three.js blends an opaque material with additive or multiply blending too. A mask's cut edges are smoothed by default; `alphaToCoverage: false` keeps three.js's hard edges.

The engine blends in linear color before the tone mapping, as `WebGPURenderer` does. `WebGLRenderer` blends after its tone mapping and sRGB encoding. So see-through surfaces look a little lighter in null3D, and additive glows a little weaker. A blended material writes depth by default, as three.js's transparent materials do. Set `depthWrite: false` on glows and on surfaces that cross, so they never hide each other.

entries.target: alphaMode: 'blend' with blending: 'weighted' on each material that the pass blended, or the quality setting momentTransparency: true for the better layer
entries.notes: The same weighted blended order-independent transparency applies, with three.js's default weight. three.js's pass takes every transparent material of normal blending without transmission; null3D takes the materials that ask for it. The weighted surfaces blend over the other see-through surfaces, test the scene's depth and write none, and `weightNode` has no counterpart.
entries.details:
The coverage sums `-log2(1 - alpha)` instead of multiplying `1 - alpha`, so both targets blend alike. Compatibility mode needs that; the result is the same. The layer draws at one sample on every path, where three.js's matches the scene's samples on WebGPU. Custom materials do not take it.

The quality setting `momentTransparency` blends the same surfaces with a store of four depth moments. That is nearer an exact back-to-front blend than the weighted average is, and it draws them twice. It is off on every preset. It takes the standard, basic and sprite materials whose blending is normal or weighted.

entries.target: doubleSided: true
entries.notes: A back face lights as if it faced the camera, as in three.js. A double-sided material with `alphaMode: 'blend'` draws its back faces first, then its front faces, as three.js does. `BackSide` has no equivalent: flip the geometry.
entries.details: `side` is fixed when the material is created.

entries.target: forceSinglePass: true
entries.notes: With alphaMode: 'blend' and doubleSided: true, both faces draw in one draw, in the mesh's triangle order. Fixed when the material is created.

entries.target: alphaMode: 'mask', alphaCutoff (alphaToCoverage is on by default)
entries.notes: The cut edges fade over one pixel above the cutoff, and MSAA covers that share of each pixel, as in three.js. null3D turns it on for every mask; `alphaToCoverage: false` turns it off. Without MSAA it is a plain mask.
entries.details: Without `alphaTest`, three.js turns raw alpha into coverage: use `alphaMode: 'hash'` for that look. A custom material takes it too, where its WGSL sets or reads the surface's alpha. Its shadow caster then keeps the mask's holes. The mode is fixed when the material is created. Its shadow cuts at `alphaCutoff`, where three.js's shadow cuts at 0.5.

entries.target: alphaMode: 'hash'
entries.notes: Three.js's cells and threshold apply to each point's place on the mesh, so the alpha sets the share of the surface that draws. The noise pattern differs: null3D hashes each cell with integer math, so every GPU draws the same pattern. `alphaCutoff` has no effect in this mode.
entries.details: three.js's sine hash changes from GPU to GPU. A hashed surface casts a hashed shadow, where three.js casts the whole shape. A custom material takes the mode where its WGSL sets or reads the surface's alpha, and its shadow and motion keep the same pattern.

entries.target: materials.standard({ wireframe: true }), and the same option on unlit and custom materials
entries.notes: Each triangle's edges draw as lines one pixel wide with the material's own shading, from an edge list that the engine keeps for each mesh. Its shadows draw lines too. Flat shading and bump maps have no effect, as in three.js, and `wireframeLinewidth` has none either.
entries.details: The option is fixed when the material is created.

entries.target: scene.setEnvironment(env); materials.standard({ envIntensity })
entries.notes: One environment lights the scene; a material takes no environment of its own. envMapIntensity becomes `envIntensity`, which multiplies the scene's intensity. three.js uses scene.environmentIntensity in place of envMapIntensity under scene.environment.

entries.target: Nothing to do
entries.notes: Options that change the shader or the pipeline, such as texture maps, vertexColors, doubleSided and flatShading, are fixed when a material is created. Create each variant during loading: a new one compiles a pipeline, which can make a frame late.

entries.target: materials.shadowCatcher({ color, opacity })
entries.notes: The plane shows the main directional light's shadow in the material's color where the shadow falls, and nothing where the light reaches it. The default color is black, as three.js's. Create the mesh with `receiveShadows: true`, or call `setReceiveShadows(true)`.
entries.details: Point and spot light shadows do not show on it. The scene's fog leaves it alone. Put the plane just above the surface whose shadows it catches.

entries.target: fog: false in the material options
materials.standard({ bumpMap, bumpScale })
entries.notes: The same formula applies: the red channel's change from one pixel to the next bends the normal. The look is the same, and it depends on the surface's size on screen as three.js's does. A normal map wins over it, as in three.js, and `bumpScale` changes with `set`.
entries.details: A normal map converted offline costs less at run time: `bunx @null3d/cli assets normal-from-bump bump.png normal.ktx2 --scale <bumpScale>`.

entries.target: materials.standard({ displacementMap, displacementScale, displacementBias })
entries.notes: Vertices move as in three.js: along the normal by the red channel times the scale, plus the bias, after skinning and morph targets. Shadows and the depth prepass follow, and culling grows each object's bounds by the farthest move. No `setBounds` call is needed.
entries.details: Without a `normalMap` or `bumpMap`, null3D bends the normals by the map's slope, so the light follows the moved surface. three.js keeps the flat mesh's normals, so a displaced surface without a normal map shades as if it were flat. With a normal map, both engines light it the same. `parallax: true` adds parallax occlusion mapping from the same map, which three.js does not have. Raycasts see the mesh before the map moves it, in both engines.

entries.target: Alpha packed into the base color map's alpha channel offline, or a surface function that sets s.alpha from the texture
entries.notes: three.js reads the alpha map from its green channel. Copy that channel into the base color map's alpha, and set alphaMode to 'mask' or 'blend'.

entries.target: A surface function with alphaMode 'mask' that sets alpha to 0 beyond the plane, using input.worldPosition
entries.notes: Pass the plane as a `vec4f` uniform. The shadow is cut at the plane too, as three.js does with `clipShadows: true`. A masked material's shadow caster runs the alpha that its surface function sets.
entries.details: three.js's default is `clipShadows: false`, which keeps the whole shadow. For that, also declare `fn coverage(input: SurfaceInput) -> f32` and return 1.0. The shadow caster then tests the coverage in place of the alpha.

entries.target: depthBias: { constant, slopeScale } in the material options
entries.notes: depthBias.constant takes polygonOffsetUnits, and depthBias.slopeScale takes polygonOffsetFactor. Signs differ because WebGPU uses reversed depth: the engine converts, so keep the three.js intent (push away from the camera).

entries.three: material.lightMap / lightMapIntensity, with the light map texture's offset and repeat
entries.target: materials.standard({ lightMap, lightMapIntensity, lightMapOffset, lightMapRepeat })
entries.notes: The light map adds baked light to the ambient light, times `lightMapIntensity`. The texture's offset and repeat become `lightMapOffset` and `lightMapRepeat`, fixed when the material is created. The engine computes `uv × repeat + offset` for the light map alone, and the other maps keep their transform.
entries.details: Load the map with `uvSet: 1` where three.js sets its channel to 1. A material with a clear coat, a sheen, iridescence or anisotropy takes no light map.

entries.target: toneMapped: false in the material's options, fixed when the material is created
entries.notes: The material keeps its display color on both paths. The 8-bit path handles it in the material's shader; the HDR path's final pass reads a mask. For the exact color on a blended surface, use the 8-bit path with `hdr: false`.

entries.target: await assets.loadTexture(url, { colorSpace, flipY, wrap, filter, mipmaps, anisotropy, uvSet, premultipliedAlpha })
entries.notes: It returns a promise of the texture, which draws once its texels upload. flipY is true by default, as in three.js, and colorSpace is 'srgb'.

entries.target: colorSpace: 'srgb' for color maps, 'linear' for data maps
entries.notes: Same rule as three.js: base color and emissive maps are sRGB; normal, roughness, metalness and AO maps are linear. The default is `'srgb'` for images and `'linear'` for data. glTF models set them automatically.
entries.details: `NoColorSpace` and `LinearSRGBColorSpace` become `colorSpace: 'linear'`.

entries.target: flipY in the loadTexture options
entries.notes: The default is true, as in three.js. A KTX2 file takes no flipY: true, so encode it flipped. glTF textures never flip.

entries.three: wrapS / wrapT / repeat / offset / rotation / center
entries.target: wrap: 'repeat' | 'clamp' | 'mirror' in the texture options; repeat, offset and rotation go in the material's uvTransform
entries.notes: `uvTransform` takes three.js's repeat, offset and rotation with the default center, and places every map of the material with it. `mapUvTransforms` gives one map, by its option name such as `emissiveMap`, a transform of its own. A glTF file's transforms stay per map.
entries.details: The default wrap is `'clamp'`, as three.js's default is `ClampToEdgeWrapping`.

entries.target: filter: 'linear' | 'nearest', mipmaps, anisotropy (capped by the preset)
textures.fromData({ width, height, depth, format, data })
entries.notes: `textures.fromData` takes `rgba8unorm` and `rgba16float` data. A depth above 1 makes a texture array, and the standard materials read its first layer. Filters are linear by default, where three.js's `DataTexture` is nearest: pass `filter: 'nearest'`.
entries.details:
A custom material declares an array as `var name: texture_2d_array<f32>` and samples a layer with `textureSample(name, nameSampler, uv, layer)`. `rgba16float` takes a `Uint16Array` of half floats or a `Float32Array`.

A `Data3DTexture` made as a color grading table for `LUTPass` becomes `assets.lutFromData({ size, data })`. Data textures have no mip levels unless `mipmaps` is true, as `DataTexture`'s `generateMipmaps` is false.

entries.three: CanvasTexture (a 2D canvas redrawn at run time)
entries.target: Draw on an OffscreenCanvas in the sketch, then textures.fromCanvas(canvas, { refreshHz }) and texture.refresh(rect)
entries.notes: The sketch worker has no DOM canvas; `OffscreenCanvas` with a 2D context works in workers. The canvas's last row goes to `v = 0`, so it stands upright on a plane, as three.js shows a `CanvasTexture`. `refresh` uploads only the rectangle, where three.js's `needsUpdate` uploads the whole canvas.
entries.details: Ask for the 2D context with `willReadFrequently: true`, so the browser keeps the pixels where the engine reads them.

entries.target: engine.registerVideo(video, { name }) on the page, then textures.fromVideo(name) in the sketch
entries.notes: A video element lives on the page, where it plays with its own controls and sound. The page sends each presented frame, scaled down to `maxSize`, and the sketch uploads the newest one within the frame's budget. A paused video presents no frame, so it costs nothing.
entries.details: The sketch's call then sends the frame that the video holds. Keep a frame within the upload budget, 2 MiB on Low: 512 texels of a 16:9 video is 576 KiB. Safari and Firefox cannot make a `VideoFrame` from a video element. So every browser reads frames through `createImageBitmap`.

entries.target: assets.loadCubemap([px, nx, py, ny, pz, nz]) for sky boxes with scene.setBackground; assets.loadEnvironment for lighting
entries.notes: The faces come in three.js's order and draw as three.js draws a `CubeTexture` background, mirrored across x. Each face is square, of one size, at most 2,048 pixels a side. A cube map does not light materials and does not blur.
entries.details: For `envMap` or a blurred background, load an environment from an HDR or EXR image with `assets.loadEnvironment`.

entries.target: await assets.loadEnvironment('sunset.hdr'), or `bunx @null3d/cli assets env sunset.hdr sunset.ktx2` and assets.loadEnvironment('sunset.ktx2')
entries.notes: One call loads a Radiance (.hdr) or OpenEXR (.exr) file and prefilters it on the GPU, as `HDRLoader` or `EXRLoader` with `PMREMGenerator.fromEquirectangular` do. No loader object and no generator to dispose. The tool's file skips the filtering at load.
entries.details: `UltraHDRLoader`'s JPEG files with gain maps do not load: convert them to .hdr or .exr. EXR files with DWAA or DWAB compression, tiled or multi-part EXR files, do not load either.

entries.target: assets.loadTexture('x.ktx2')
entries.notes: The engine loads the transcoder with the first KTX2 file and picks the device's format, so delete the setup. The file's first row is at `v = 0`, as with `KTX2Loader`. UASTC HDR files load too: as BC6H where the device has BC formats, else as `rgb9e5ufloat`.
entries.details: three.js uses ASTC HDR or half floats there. Both stay linear, so keep tone mapping on. The engine keeps each transcoded texture in its cache of derived data, so a repeat visit skips the transcoder. `KTX2Loader` transcodes on every visit.

entries.target: assets.loadTexture('x.ktx2'); texture.format names the compressed format
entries.notes: Compressed textures come from KTX2 files of ETC1S or UASTC data, with the file's mip levels. No call takes compressed blocks from code.

entries.three: texture.channel (which UV set a map uses)
entries.target: uvSet: 0 or 1 in the texture's options
entries.notes: Each map of a material reads the set that its texture names. glTF models carry this per texture, so loaded models need nothing.

entries.target: loadTexture(url, { premultipliedAlpha: true }), which multiplies each color by its alpha as the image decodes
entries.notes: Blending needs no material flag: the engine blends premultiplied colors. On a blended material, a base color map loaded with `premultipliedAlpha: true` looks the same as one loaded without it. The shader divides its colors by their alpha before it lights them.
entries.details: Other materials show the multiplied colors, as three.js does.

entries.target: const prefab = await assets.loadGltf(url); scene.instantiate(prefab)
entries.notes: A worker parses the file, and `scene.instantiate(prefab)` makes a copy. Named nodes come from `prefab.find(name)`, a copy's objects from `instance.find(name)`, and its maps from `prefab.find(name).maps`. KTX2, WebP, AVIF and meshopt need no decoder setup.
entries.details:
`prefab.bounds` frames the model. Clips play through the copy's animator: `scene.instantiate(prefab).animator().play(name)`, with the names in `prefab.clips`. Joints are not objects. Morph targets draw, and clips animate their weights.

Materials follow `GLTFLoader`'s rules. Vertex colors turn on, a mesh without normals shades flat, and blended materials write no depth. A mesh without tangents turns the normal map's green channel over. `KHR_lights_punctual` lights load with the intensities that three.js gives them. A clip without a name is named `animation_0`, `animation_1` and so on, as three.js names it.

`KHR_animation_pointer` needs no plugin: the loader reads it. It moves the same texture transform values as three.js's plugin. `assets.registerGltfExtension(handler)` takes the place of `GLTFLoader.register()` for an add-on's extensions. `GLTFLoader` ignores the MSFT_lod levels of `bunx @null3d/cli assets optimize --lod` and draws the full mesh.

entries.target: assets.loadGltf(url, { rewriteUrl: (address) => address })
entries.notes: Checks or changes each address that a glTF file names, for its buffers and images. Return null to refuse the file with E1416. It covers glTF files only.

entries.target: Built in: assets.loadGltf(url) decodes Draco data
entries.notes: Delete the setup and the decoder files. The engine ships Draco's glTF decoder and downloads it, about 60 KB after Brotli, with the first Draco file. Convert the files to meshopt with `bunx @null3d/cli assets optimize`: meshopt files decode faster, with a decoder of about 6 KB.

entries.target: Built in: assets.loadGltf(url) decodes meshopt data
entries.notes: Delete the setup. The loader reads KHR_meshopt_compression and EXT_meshopt_compression, and downloads the decoder with the first compressed file.

entries.three: FBXLoader / OBJLoader / MTLLoader / ColladaLoader / STLLoader / PLYLoader / 3DMLoader / USDZLoader
entries.target: Convert to glTF before release: `bunx @null3d/cli assets convert model.fbx model.glb` for FBX, OBJ with MTL, STL and PLY; Blender for Collada, 3DM and USDZ
entries.notes: The engine loads glTF only. The command keeps FBX skins, blend shapes and clips, turns materials into metal-rough ones, and puts units in meters with Y up. Bump maps become normal maps.
entries.details: The command is `bunx @null3d/cli assets convert model.fbx model.glb` for FBX, OBJ with MTL, STL and PLY; Blender handles Collada, 3DM and USDZ. The engine draws no glTF points, so a converted PLY point cloud loads with nothing to draw. three.js draws it.

entries.target: assets.onProgress((loaded, total) => ...) and assets.preload([...urls])
entries.notes: `loaded` and `total` count bytes, not files. A download that announces no length still adds its bytes to `loaded`, while `total` stays unknown. Divide by `Math.max(total, loaded)`.

entries.target: assets.loadBinary(url), assets.loadJson(url), assets.loadImageBitmap(url)
entries.notes: ImageBitmapLoader's texture becomes textures.fromImageBitmap, which puts the bitmap's first row at v = 0. assets.loadImageBitmap flips the rows by default, as createImageBitmap does with imageOrientation: 'flipY', so the texture stands upright, as three.js's TextureLoader shows it.

entries.target: Nothing to do
entries.notes: Loads of one URL at the same time share one download. Files that `assets.preload` downloaded wait in memory until a load takes them. The HTTP cache keeps the rest.

entries.target: scene.createInstances(mesh, count, { material, dynamic, colors }); write batch.positions / rotations / scales / colors
entries.notes: Static batches call `markDirty(start, count)` after writes; dynamic batches upload every frame without it. `colors: true` adds the colors array: linear RGBA per row, which multiplies the base color and opacity. `scene.createInstances(prefab, count)` instances a glTF model, with one set of rows for all its meshes.
entries.details: `setColorAt`'s color works the same as a row color. `castShadow` and `receiveShadow` become `castShadows` and `receiveShadows`, or `batch.setCastShadows` and `setReceiveShadows`. An `InstancedMesh`'s `boundingSphere` becomes `batch.setBoundingRadius(radius)` for that batch. Each row's sphere then holds that radius around the row's origin.

entries.target: Nothing special: the engine batches objects that share a mesh and material
entries.notes: Use createInstances for many copies of one mesh, and separate meshes for varied geometry.

entries.target: createInstances(mesh, count, { material, values: true }) adds batch.values, four floats per row, which a custom material's vertexOffset and surface functions read as object.values
entries.notes: Four floats per row replace named attributes: pack a phase, an age, a tint or a size into them. A shader that read an instanced attribute reads object.values.x to .w instead. A material with a vertexOffset casts shadows that follow it.

entries.three: A BufferGeometry with no attributes, drawn from a vertex count in a ShaderMaterial (gl_VertexID and gl_InstanceID)
entries.target: scene.createVertexDraw({ shader, vertices, instances, bounds, ...material options })
entries.notes: The shader makes every vertex from `@builtin(vertex_index)` and `@builtin(instance_index)`, so a frame uploads nothing. three.js needs a geometry with a placeholder attribute and an `InstancedBufferGeometry` for the instance count. A draw blends, sorts as one object, takes no texture, casts no shadow, and a raycast does not hit its shapes.

entries.target: Nothing for a mesh made in code of 4,096 triangles or more, or of 256 or more whose copies hold 65,536: it plans its levels on the job workers at its first draw, and `await mesh.buildLevels()` plans another; or baseMesh.setLevels([{ mesh, distance }]) on the base mesh, then draw the base mesh; or levels from `bunx @null3d/cli assets optimize --lod`, which assets.loadGltf reads
entries.notes: Levels belong to the mesh, and each object and instance row picks its own level each frame. It measures to the nearest point of an object's bounds, where three.js measures to its position, so a large object switches later. `getCurrentLevel` and `autoUpdate` have no match.
entries.details:
A mesh made in code plans measured levels with the asset tool's planner, as three.js's `SimplifyModifier` would make far copies by hand. They switch at once while the threshold stays small. `levels: false` in its arrays opts out.

Each object and row picks its level on the GPU or on job workers, by the level's error, distance or screen coverage. A distance holds on every screen height, and so does a coverage. A hand-set level fades over a dithered band, which replaces hysteresis. A level with a measured error switches at once while the threshold stays small, and fades above about one and a half pixels. A mesh whose bound covers fewer pixels than the threshold draws nothing.
