Each shadow map picks a caster's level in its own texels, so the level holds while the camera moves. A level may name a material of its own, so a far level shades more cheaply.

`object.setLevelBias(bias)` moves one object's threshold, as Godot's `lod_bias` does. Above 1 it draws coarser levels, and below 1 it keeps more detail. `object.setDrawRange(start, end)` draws a mesh only inside a band of distances, and fades it at each edge.

Far copies can also draw as impostor cards or as one merged mesh per far cell, from `@null3d/impostors`. The cards blend the three nearest stored views and light from the normals the bake stores. So a moving sun relights them with the meshes.

A large static mesh can also take a tree of cluster patches from `bunx @null3d/cli assets optimize --clusters`. The engine then draws fine patches near the camera and coarse ones far from it. It does so on both GPU paths where the browser draws many ranges in one call, and whole levels elsewhere. three.js has no equivalent, and its LOD picks one level for the whole object.

entries.three: AnimationMixer / clipAction / play / crossFadeTo / fadeIn / fadeOut / time / setEffectiveWeight / timeScale / mixer.update(dt)
entries.target: const anim = obj.animator(); anim.play('run', { fade: 0.2, loop: true, speed: 1 }); anim.crossFade('walk', 0.3); anim.play('walk', { time: 0.4, weight: 0.7 }); anim.setWeight('walk', 0.5); anim.setLayerWeight(1, 0.5); anim.setTimeScale(0.5); anim.onEvent('finished', handler)
entries.notes: No update call: the engine advances and blends every animator on its job workers. `action.time = t` before `play()` becomes `play(name, { time: t })`. `setLoop(LoopOnce)` becomes `loop: false`, which holds the last frame, as `clampWhenFinished` does; `startAt` has no counterpart.
entries.details:
`setEffectiveWeight(w)` on actions that play together becomes `play(name, { weight: w })`, then `setWeight(name, w)`. A play with a weight joins its layer's clips, and a play without one fades them out. `setWeight` leaves a running fade in place, which multiplies the weight. A fade out starts from the clip's current weight, not from full weight.

`fadeOut(duration)` becomes `stop(name, { fade: duration })`. A clip with a negative speed starts at its end. Filtered clips for upper and lower body become layers with `setLayerMask`. Walk and run blends become `playBlend` and `setBlend`, which keep the clips in step. This covers blends whose weights and time scales the code works out from a speed.

`crossFadeTo` and `crossFadeFrom` map to `crossFade`, which keeps the weighted blend that three.js shows. It never uses an inertial transition, which samples only the new clip. `startAt` has no direct call: call `play` at that time. `mixer.addEventListener('loop' or 'finished')` becomes `anim.onEvent('loop' or 'finished', handler)`, which also gets the events in the clip's data. Handlers run at the start of the next frame, before `onUpdate`. So code sees what the clips reached in the frame before, as after `mixer.update`.

A clip blends only where it has tracks, as in three.js. Poses, fades, masked layers, additive clips and blends match three.js's within 0.0004. A clip whose keys follow no single grid is stored at 30 keys per second. Its fastest joints can then cut corners by up to 0.005.

entries.target: const pulse = scene.animateProperty(lamp, 'light.intensity', { times: [0, 1, 2], values: [0, 5, 0], loop: true }); const recolor = scene.animateProperty(material, 'color', { times: [0, 1], values: [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1] })
entries.notes: A track names a value of a light, a camera, a material or an object. Keys hold one number, two for a map's offset or scale, three for a color, position or scale, and four for a rotation. glTF files play their `KHR_animation_pointer` tracks through the model's animator.
entries.details:
The values include `'light.intensity'`, `'light.color'`, `'camera.fov'`, a material value that `setUniform` takes, `'material.uvOffset'` or `'material.uvScale'`, and `'position'`, `'rotation'`, `'scale'` and `'visible'`.

Interpolation is `'linear'`, `'step'` or glTF's cubic spline (`'cubic'`). A cubic key holds an in-tangent, the value and an out-tangent. `animation.setTime(t)` places the animation. `setSpeed`, `setPaused`, `setLoop` and `stop` control it. A material animation changes every object that uses the material.

The glTF tracks carry the clip's time, speed, fades and weights. They cover a light's intensity, color and range, a material's values, and the offset and scale of a base color or emissive texture's transform. They also cover a node's visibility, and a node's transform or morph weights.

A material keeps a transform for each of its maps, so a file that moves two of them apart plays both. Each plays on its own map. A pointer the engine does not read leaves its value as the file has it, with a warning in development builds. three.js needs a plugin for the extension.

entries.three: SkinnedMesh / Skeleton / Bone built by hand
entries.target: Author the skeleton in a modeling tool and export glTF: const hero = scene.instantiate(await assets.loadGltf(url)); hero.animator().play('walk')
entries.notes: Building skeletons in code is not supported, and joints are not objects. Meshes that hang on bones, such as a sword in a hand, follow their joints when the file puts them under the bone. To turn a joint from code, use the animator's joint calls (see the bone rotation entry).
entries.details: The mesh's own world matrix places the skinned vertices, as three.js draws a `SkinnedMesh`. Each pass skins the mesh in its vertex shader, as three.js does, custom materials included.

entries.three: bone.quaternion / bone.rotation set after mixer.update(dt); bone.lookAt(target); skeleton.getBoneByName
entries.target: const head = anim.joint('Head'); anim.setJointRotation(head, q, weight); anim.addJointRotation(head, q, weight); anim.lookAt(target, { joints: ['Spine', 'Neck', 'Head'], limit }, weight)
entries.notes: Setting `bone.quaternion` after the mixer's update becomes `setJointRotation`, and multiplying it becomes `addJointRotation`, which turns the joint in its own frame. Turn a `bone.rotation` Euler into a quaternion with `quat.fromEuler` first. Both take a weight from 0 to 1 that blends with the animated rotation.
entries.details: A rotation holds in every frame until `clearJoint`, where three.js's mixer overwrites the bone in its next update. `bone.lookAt` becomes `lookAt`, which turns a chain of up to 4 joints toward a point in the world. Each turns within its limit, and it aims again every frame until `lookAt(null)`. The joints below follow, so a held rifle aims with the arms.

entries.target: anim.play(name, { additive: true }) for makeClipAdditive. Split clips for subclip in the modeling tool
entries.notes: An additive play adds the clip's change from its first frame, as makeClipAdditive does with its default reference frame. The engine makes the additive form once, at the first additive play.

entries.target: camera.screenToRay(x, y, ray); scene.raycast(ray.origin, ray.direction, { layers }, hit)
entries.notes: `scene.raycast` writes the closest hit into a hit object that you create once, and `scene.raycastAll` writes every hit, nearest first. A layer mask defaults to layer 0 alone, as `Raycaster`'s does, and hidden objects are never hit. A skinned mesh is tested in its bind pose, not its animated pose.
entries.details:
A hit has `object`, `instance` (`instanceId`), `point`, `normal`, `distance` and `triangle` (`faceIndex`). It also has `uv` (`intersection.uv`) with `hasUv`, which says whether the hit triangle has texture coordinates. `camera.screenToRay` uses the camera of the frame on screen at the pointer's event. For clicks and hover on objects, `obj.on('click', fn)` casts the ray itself. Acceleration structures are built in. Rays hit sprites, points and lines as they draw.

`raycaster.far` becomes `maxDistance`. `params.Points.threshold` and `params.Line.threshold` become the `pointThreshold` and `lineThreshold` options. three.js gives both a default of 1 world unit, and null3D none. Without them, a ray hits a point's square, or a line within half its width. A hit near a line, or near a point within a threshold, is the ray's closest point. three.js puts a `Line`'s hit on the line instead.

Triangles hit as their material draws them, front faces only or both with `doubleSided: true`, as `Raycaster` reads `material.side`. A ray hits a dashed line's gaps, and a sprite or point where its map is clear, as in three.js. `scene.pick(x, y)` tests the pixel that the image shows, through the GPU, and returns a promise. three.js has no pixel pick.

Sprites, points and lines sized in pixels use the active camera, or the camera of the event's frame, in place of `raycaster.camera`. three.js's `Line2` and `LineSegments2` ignore `raycaster.far`; `maxDistance` limits every null3D hit, lines too.

entries.three: DOM pointer, mouse, touch and keyboard listeners
entries.target: input.pointer, input.isDown('KeyW'), input.wasPressed('Mouse0'), input.touches, input.actions.define(); obj.on('click' | 'pointerdown' | 'pointerup' | 'pointermove' | 'pointerenter' | 'pointerleave', fn)
entries.notes: The page forwards pointer, touch, keyboard and gamepad input to the sketch, which reads it once per frame and adds no DOM listeners. Keys take `KeyboardEvent.code` names, and the main mouse button or a tap is `Mouse0`. A canvas that takes touch gestures needs `touch-action: none` in its CSS.
entries.details: `obj.on` replaces a canvas listener that raycasts: the closest object under the pointer gets the event, then its parents. `input.pointer.wheel` gives the scroll in pixels, counting a line as 16 pixels and a page as 100, as three.js's controls count `deltaMode`.

entries.target: createOrbitControls(ctx, camera, { target, enableDamping, dampingFactor, minDistance, maxDistance, maxPolarAngle }) or createMapControls(ctx, camera) from @null3d/controls; controls.update(dt) in onUpdate
entries.notes: Option names and defaults match `OrbitControls` and `MapControls`, and the same input gives the camera the same pose. `mouseButtons` and `touches` take strings such as `'rotate'` and `'dolly-pan'`. There is no DOM element, so `connect`, `disconnect` and `dispose` have no equivalent.
entries.details:
`listenToKeyEvents()` takes no element: it turns on the keys, which the sketch's `input` already reads. There are no change, start or end events: `update(dt)` returns true when the camera moved.

`zoomToCursor`, `keys`, `keyPanSpeed`, `keyRotateSpeed`, `cursor`, `minTargetRadius`, `maxTargetRadius`, `saveState` and `reset` keep three.js's names and behavior. A held key repeats after half a second, then 30 times a second, where three.js follows the system's key repeat. An orthographic camera zooms by its view height, and `minZoom` and `maxZoom` count zoom as three.js does from the height when the controls start. `getDistance`, `getPolarAngle` and `getAzimuthalAngle` keep three.js's meaning. `rotateLeft`, `rotateUp`, `pan`, `dollyIn` and `dollyOut` take effect at the next update, not at once.

`dampingFactor` is the share at 60 frames per second. The engine scales it to each frame's step, so the motion takes the same time at any frame rate. The controls orbit around +Y, where three.js orbits around the camera's up. three.js takes a frame's events one at a time, so a two-finger pan can differ by a few percent of the move.

entries.target: None; createOrbitControls, or your own rotation from ctx.input
entries.notes: null3D has orbit and map controls. It has no trackball or arcball rotation.

entries.target: createFlyControls(ctx, camera, { movementSpeed, rollSpeed, dragToLook, autoForward }) or createFirstPersonControls(ctx, camera, { movementSpeed, lookSpeed, pointerSpeed, minPolarAngle, maxPolarAngle }) from @null3d/controls; controls.update(dt) in onUpdate
entries.notes: Option names and defaults match `FlyControls`, `FirstPersonControls` and `PointerLockControls`. First-person controls take the place of the last two: while the canvas holds the pointer lock, the mouse turns the view as `PointerLockControls` turn it. `lock()`, `unlock()` and `isLocked` have no equivalent.
entries.details:
The page asks for the lock in a click handler with `engine.requestPointerLock()`, and the sketch reads `input.pointer.locked`. For code that moves the camera itself, set `movementSpeed: 0` and call `controls.moveForward` and `controls.moveRight`. There is no DOM element, dispose or change event: `update(dt)` returns true when the camera moved.

In fly controls, the keys add to the pointer's turn, where three.js's pointer replaces the arrow keys' turn. First-person controls turn the camera with no roll, where `PointerLockControls` keep a roll the camera had. With the pointer locked, a frame's mouse moves add up before the polar limits apply.

three.js applies the limits after each move, so a frame can end at a different angle. With two fingers down, the first finger turns the view, where three.js follows the finger that touched down last. `dampingFactor` is the share at 60 frames per second, scaled to each frame's step.

entries.target: createTransformControls(ctx, camera, { mode, space, size, showX, showY, showZ, translationSnap, rotationSnap, scaleSnap }) from @null3d/controls, then attach(object) and controls.update(dt) in onUpdate; createDragControls(ctx, camera, objects, { recursive, transformGroup, rotateSpeed, mouseButtons, touches })
entries.notes: Option names and defaults match `TransformControls` and `DragControls`. There is no DOM element, `getHelper` or event: the controls make their handles in the scene and report `dragging`, `axis`, `hovered` and `state`. `update(dt)` returns true when it moved something.
entries.details:
A gizmo turns an object by the exact angle that the pointer sweeps around the axis, where three.js scales a linear approximation of it. `minX` to `maxZ` clamp a move, and `showXY`, `showYZ` and `showXZ` hide the plane handles, as in three.js. `showX`, `showY` and `showZ` hide the plane handles too. A press on a handle reaches the handle alone, so a click handler on the object behind it does not hear it.

`dragging` and `axis` replace `TransformControls`' dragging-changed, objectChange, mouseDown and mouseUp events. `dragging`, `hovered` and `state` replace `DragControls`' dragstart, drag, dragend, hoveron and hoveroff events.

entries.three: AxesHelper / GridHelper / BoxHelper / Box3Helper / ArrowHelper / CameraHelper / light helpers / SkeletonHelper / PlaneHelper
entries.target: debug.axes, debug.grid, debug.box, debug.sphere, debug.arrow, debug.frustum, debug.light, debug.skeleton
entries.notes: Call them in `onUpdate`: each call draws for one frame, and debug drawing exists in development builds only. `debug.grid` takes `GridHelper`'s size and divisions, and its `color` and `centerColor` default to `GridHelper`'s `color2` and `color1`. `PlaneHelper` and `PolarGridHelper` have no equivalent.
entries.details: `debug.frustum` draws orange by default, as `CameraHelper` draws a frustum. `debug.box` takes a box's lowest and highest corners. `debug.light` draws directional lights only. `debug.skeleton` draws an animated object's skin joints, blue at the joint and green at its parent, as `SkeletonHelper` does.

entries.three: three.js's Inspector add-on or developer tools extension, or code that walks scene.children to find an object while debugging
entries.target: ?inspect on the page in a development build; engine.inspect(call, args) from page code; bunx @null3d/cli mcp for a coding agent
entries.notes: The `?inspect` panel lists the scene as a tree and outlines the object that you select. It shows and changes the object's transform, and a mesh's base color, roughness, metalness and opacity. A change lasts until the page reloads, so copy the final values into the sketch.
entries.details: `engine.inspect` runs the same calls from code, and the page answers capture itself with `{ png, bytes }`. The MCP server gives a coding agent the same calls, frame captures and the frame figures. All three work in a development build only, because a production build leaves the channel out. A held page or a replay opens no panel.

entries.three: new Vector3 / Quaternion / Matrix4 / Euler / Color / Box3 / Sphere / Ray / Plane
entries.target: Plain arrays and the vec3, quat, mat4 and color helpers from @null3d/engine, such as vec3.add(out, a, b) and quat.slerp(out, a, b, t)
entries.notes: Create scratch arrays once with `vec3.create()`, `quat.create()` or `mat4.create()`, outside `onUpdate`. Most names match three.js, and each helper does three.js's arithmetic, so the results match. Coordinates are right-handed with +Y up, as in three.js.
entries.details:
A `mat4` holds its 16 numbers column by column, as `Matrix4.elements` does, with the translation in elements 12, 13 and 14. `multiplyMatrices(a, b)` is `mat4.multiply(out, a, b)`, and `multiplyQuaternions(a, b)` is `quat.multiply(out, a, b)`. Both apply b first, then a. `setFromRotationMatrix(m)` is `quat.fromMat4(out, m)`, which needs a matrix without scale. Use `mat4.decompose` for one with scale.

`applyQuaternion` is `vec3.transformQuat`, `applyMatrix4` is `vec3.transformMat4`, `multiplyScalar` is `vec3.scale`, and `addScaledVector` is `vec3.scaleAndAdd`. `setFromUnitVectors` is `quat.rotationTo`, and `setFromEuler` is `quat.fromEuler`, in radians. There are no helpers for `Box3`, `Sphere`, `Ray` or `Plane`.

three.js math classes may stay in setup code during a port, but not in per-frame code. Game rules that a server replays import the exact helpers from `@null3d/engine/math/vec3`, `quat`, `mat4` and `math`. They build `setAxisAngle`, `fromEuler`, `rotateX`, `rotateY`, `rotateZ`, `slerp`, `vec3.angle` and `math.damp` with `createMath` on an exact math library.

entries.target: onUpdate(dt) or ctx.time.dt, and ctx.time.now
entries.notes: getDelta() becomes the dt that onUpdate gets, also in ctx.time.dt, and getElapsedTime() becomes ctx.time.now. Sketch time stops while the engine is paused or the page is hidden. A fixed-step simulation, such as world.step(1 / 60), moves to onFixedUpdate.

entries.three: MathUtils (degToRad, clamp, lerp, damp, randFloat, seededRandom)
entries.target: math.degToRad, radToDeg, clamp, lerp, inverseLerp, mapLinear, damp, smoothstep, euclideanModulo, randFloat, randInt and randFloatSpread; math.seed and math.random
entries.notes: Same names and arithmetic, and the random helpers draw from `math.random`, which hold mode seeds. `MathUtils.seededRandom(s)` becomes `math.seed(s)` once, then `math.random()`. `smootherstep`, `pingpong` and `generateUUID` have no equivalent.
entries.details: Game rules that a server replays import `clamp`, `lerp` and the other exact helpers from `@null3d/engine/math/math`. They build `damp` with `createMath` on an exact math library, and draw random numbers from a generator of their own.

entries.target: '#rrggbb' or '#rgb' strings, 0xrrggbb numbers, or [r, g, b] linear arrays from 0 to 1; color.fromHex, color.fromSrgb and color.fromHsl give linear RGB
entries.notes: Hex values are sRGB, as `setHex` and `setStyle` read them, and the engine converts them to linear. `[r, g, b]` arrays are linear, as `setRGB` reads them, so the color helpers' results go straight into color options and instance colors. `color.fromSrgb` converts sRGB components, `color.fromHsl` gives what `setHSL` gives, and `vec3.lerp` blends two colors.
entries.details: `color.srgbToLinear` and `color.linearToSrgb` convert one component by the same curve as `SRGBToLinear` and `LinearToSRGB`.

entries.three: EffectComposer / RenderPass / OutputPass / PostProcessing (three/webgpu) / pmndrs postprocessing
entries.target: post.set({ ... })
entries.notes: The chain is built in and merged into few passes. Delete the composer, RenderPass and OutputPass; keep only each pass's settings.

entries.target: post.set({ bloom: { intensity, threshold, knee, blend, weights } })
entries.notes: null3D draws bloom through a chain of mip levels, so the settings map rather than copy. `UnrealBloomPass` uses `blend: 'add'`, the same threshold, knee 0.01, and intensity about 8.8 times strength. Take weights from radius with the port skill's table, or its `map-bloom.mjs` script for the app's canvas size.
entries.details:
The `bloom()` node is the same at a third of the intensity. pmndrs `BloomEffect` uses `blend: 'screen'`, intensity as is, `threshold` from `luminanceThreshold` and `knee` from `luminanceSmoothing`. Its weights come from radius and levels. Drop the resolution argument.

The match holds at one canvas size, 1080 pixels on the shorter side by default. three.js's glow spans pixels, so on a larger screen null3D's looks wider. A strong bloom also spreads a little wider at the frame's edges than three.js's. three.js's faint haze fades toward the corners; lower strength or radius to soften it. In WebGPU's compatibility mode with MSAA, bloom moves the engine to HDR color with FXAA.

entries.target: post.set({ ao: { radius, thickness, distanceExponent, distanceFalloff, scale, samples, intensity } })
entries.notes: `GTAOPass`'s search and denoise draw at half resolution, with its setting names. `blendIntensity` becomes `intensity`, and `distanceFallOff` is spelled `distanceFalloff`. It darkens only the ambient light, where `GTAOPass` darkens the whole image.
entries.details:
It draws where the quality setting `aoScale` is above 0: on High and Ultra, or after `quality.set({ aoScale: 0.5 })` on phones and tablets. For `SSAOPass`, `SAOPass` and `N8AO`, start from the defaults and tune `radius` and `scale` by eye.

In the engine's parity tests with `GTAOPass`'s defaults, under 0.1% of the pixels differ from three.js's image on every GPU path. With a wider, darker search, under 1% differ, along the soft edges. A scene that only ambient light lights gives the same image in both.

entries.three: SSGINode / ssgi() (bounce light from the screen) / VXGINode
entries.target: A light probe grid for bounce light (scene.setLightProbeGrid), with ambient occlusion (post.set({ ao }))
entries.notes: null3D has no bounce light from the screen and no voxel cone tracing. The probe grid gives colored bounce light everywhere, from objects off the screen too, at a fixed cost per pixel. Light from moving objects reaches it only when the sketch bakes it again.

entries.target: createEngine({ antialias: 'fxaa' }); the quality presets take MSAA 4x from Medium, and FXAA on Low
entries.notes: FXAA runs inside the final pass, where three.js adds `FXAAPass` after `OutputPass`. null3D has no TAA of a moving view. A still view blends jittered frames into a sharper picture, then rests, so TAA and SSAA passes have no counterpart.
entries.details: SMAA 1x smooths the moment transparency layer's edges under the share that its moments cover. The rest of the image keeps MSAA's samples or FXAA. `sampleLevel` has no counterpart. The motion debug view reads the motion vectors that the engine records for each object.

entries.target: MSAA, which the quality presets take from Medium up, with FXAA on Low
entries.notes: null3D has no temporal anti-aliasing and no temporal upscaler. Drop the node and keep the scene's MSAA, which `TAAUNode` had to turn off. For speed on phones, the governor lowers the render scale, and the final pass scales the image up.

entries.target: The render scale: quality.set({ minRenderScale, maxRenderScale })
entries.notes: The engine draws the scene below the canvas size when the render scale is under 1. Its final pass scales the image up with GSR 1, an edge-aware spatial upscaler, which fills FSR 1's role. It has no FSR 1 pass.
entries.details: Sharpening is a setting of its own, `post.set({ sharpen })`, which draws at the whole canvas's render scale.

entries.target: post.set({ sharpen })
entries.notes: Both sharpen display color with FSR 1's RCAS in the final pass, so the port needs no render target and no pass of its own. three.js scales the sharpening by `2^-sharpness`, where 0 sharpens the most and 2 does nothing. Set `sharpen` to that factor, so three.js's default of 0.2 is `sharpen: 0.87`.
entries.details: null3D damps the sharpening where the ring around a pixel is noise, which three.js does only with `denoise: true`. It draws at the whole canvas's render scale; below one, the upscale sharpens the image itself.

entries.target: post.set({ outline: { color, hiddenColor, width } }) and mesh.setOutlined(true), or createOutlinePass(ctx, { color, hiddenColor, strength, thickness, glow, pulsePeriod }) from @null3d/three-compat
entries.notes: `selectedObjects` becomes `setOutlined(true)` on each mesh, or on a model's copy from `scene.instantiate`. null3D draws a crisp line of one width in CSS pixels, with no blur. `visibleEdgeColor` and `hiddenEdgeColor` become `color` and `hiddenColor`; the pattern texture has no setting.
entries.details:
`OutlinePass` draws its edge at half size, so `edgeThickness` t becomes `width` of about 2t. `OutlinePass` draws a dark brown line around hidden parts by default. null3D draws none until `hiddenColor` is set, so set `hiddenColor: [0.1, 0.04, 0.02]`, its linear default, to keep it.

pmndrs `OutlineEffect`: `xRay: false` becomes `hiddenColor: false`. Its edge is one texel of its mask at `resolutionScale`, so `width` is about `1 / resolutionScale`.

For `OutlinePass` itself, install `@null3d/three-compat` and call `createOutlinePass(ctx, { color, hiddenColor, strength, thickness, glow, pulsePeriod })`. `edgeStrength`, `edgeThickness` and `edgeGlow` keep their values as `strength`, `thickness` and `glow`, and `pulsePeriod` keeps its name. `visibleEdgeColor` and `hiddenEdgeColor` become `color` and `hiddenColor`. It draws the soft edge, the glow and the pulse, and it turns the crisp line off. The mask reads at half size, and `downSampleRatio` is fixed at 2. The core's crisp line stays the cheaper choice where a soft edge is not needed.

One outline style covers every outlined object in either form. For a soft glow built by hand, a full-screen pass reads the mask with `input: 'outlineMask'`, at scale 0.5. An effect then adds its texture to the scene color; `width: 0` drops the crisp line (guides/custom-passes, a soft outline glow).

entries.target: post.set({ dof: { focusDistance, focusPoint, aperture, focalLength, maxBlur, blades } }), with camera.setFocalLength(mm)
entries.notes: The same intent uses a camera's lens: the blur grows with the distance from the focus, and the near and far fields blur apart. So a sharp object spreads no halo into a blurred background. `BokehPass`'s focus becomes `focusDistance`.
entries.details:
Its aperture scales the blur with the distance from the focus. null3D's aperture is an f-number, so pick one by eye, such as 2.8, with the camera's focal length (`camera.setFocalLength`). `maxblur` is a share of the canvas's width, and `maxBlur` of its height, so multiply by the aspect ratio.

pmndrs `DepthOfFieldEffect`: `worldFocusDistance` becomes `focusDistance`, a target to focus on becomes `focusPoint`, and `bokehScale` becomes `maxBlur` with the aperture. Tune it by eye. It draws where the quality setting `dofSamples` is above 0: Medium and up, or `quality.set({ dofSamples: 16 })` on Low.

entries.three: None built in; pmndrs ToneMappingEffect with ToneMappingMode.REINHARD2_ADAPTIVE (adaptationRate, middleGrey), AdaptiveLuminancePass, AdaptiveToneMappingPass
entries.target: post.set({ autoExposure: { metering, percentiles, centerWeight, speedUp, speedDown, minEv, maxEv, compensation } })
entries.notes: three.js has no automatic exposure; `renderer.toneMappingExposure` stays `post.set({ exposure })`, and the eye adapts from it. pmndrs's adaptive tone mapping becomes `autoExposure` with `metering: 'mean'`. Its `adaptationRate` becomes about `speedUp` and `speedDown`, and its `middleGrey` the compensation, `log2(middleGrey / 0.18)` stops.
entries.details:
Its Reinhard curve becomes a custom tone curve. The meter runs on the GPU in the same frame: a histogram on WebGPU, or 16 x 16 cells on WebGL2 and the Low preset. The quality setting is `exposureMeter`.

It weights the center and adapts at its own speeds for brighter and darker scenes. It stays within `minEv` and `maxEv`, in stops from the camera's exposure. Hold mode settles at once, so image tests stay the same. It needs HDR color, as bloom does.

entries.target: post.addEffect({ wgsl, uniforms, textures, order }), or render.addPass({ kind: 'fullscreen', wgsl, writes, size or scale }) for a pass that writes a render target of its own
entries.notes: Rewrite the fragment shader in WGSL as `fn effect(input: EffectInput) -> vec4f`. `texture2D(tDiffuse, vUv)` becomes `effectColor(input.uv)`, and `pass.uniforms.x.value = v` becomes `post.setEffectUniform(effect, 'x', v)`. The engine joins effects that read only their own pixel into one pass.
entries.details:
Effects run on linear HDR color before the tone curve. A `ShaderPass` after `OutputPass` sees display color, so retune its numbers. The uv's y axis is flipped: replace `vUv.y` with `1.0 - input.uv.y` where direction matters. Other textures of the shader become `var name: texture_2d<f32>` with the `textures` option. Sample a render pass's texture at `effectPassUv(input.uv)`. A reflection pass's texture on the HDR WebGPU path starts at the top row instead: sample it at `input.uv`.

A `ShaderPass` that writes a render target of its own, which a later pass reads, becomes a full-screen pass. Its input image goes as `input: 'sceneColor'`, or a texture. `effectViewPosition(uv)` gives the surface's view-space position, whose z is negative in front of the camera, as in three.js.

entries.target: A custom effect for each, with post.addEffect
entries.notes: Port each shader as a ShaderPass is ported. Grain and noise sized for display color look weaker on HDR color, so tune them by eye. GlitchPass's random texture becomes a texture of the effect, from textures.fromData, or noise from null3d::noise.

entries.target: None
entries.notes: AfterimagePass blends in the frame before, which an effect cannot read, so it has no port.

entries.target: post.set({ lut: await assets.loadLut('grade.cube'), lutIntensity }), or a table from assets.lutFromData({ size, data })
entries.notes: `LUTPass`'s intensity becomes `lutIntensity`. The table grades display color after the tone mapping, as `LUTPass` after `OutputPass` does. A `Data3DTexture` that code fills for `LUTPass` becomes `await assets.lutFromData({ size, data })`.
entries.details:
The order is the same, red fastest, with three or four numbers per texel, whose fourth is skipped. Give floats from 0 to 1, so divide 8-bit values by 255. `LUTImageLoader`'s PNG strips are not read: export the grade as a .cube file. Both read the table with a linear filter between its texel centers.

The engine maps the colors of a .cube file's domain onto the table, which `LUTPass` leaves out. A .3dl input grid whose points differ from even steps by one loads, where `LUT3dlLoader` refuses it. In the engine's parity test, a .cube table matches three.js's composer in all but under 0.1% of the pixels on every GPU path.

entries.target: post.set({ vignette: { intensity, size, falloff, roundness } })
entries.notes: null3D's vignette multiplies HDR color before the tone mapping, so bright corners darken instead of turning gray. `VignetteShader`'s offset becomes `size` and darkness becomes `intensity`. Under ACES, the default falloff of 2 and roundness of 0 give a close match.
entries.details: Under AgX, intensity stays at 1 or less with a falloff of 3. With darkness below 1, three.js also lifts dark corners toward a gray, and null3D does not. The postprocessing library's `VignetteEffect` maps the same way with its ESKIL technique. Its default technique darkens with another curve, so tune intensity and size by eye.

entries.target: post.set({ ssr: { maxDistance, thickness, intensity } }) with quality.set({ ssrScale })
entries.notes: It reflects what the screen shows in smooth opaque surfaces, in place of the environment's reflection, through the material's Fresnel term. `SSRPass` adds its reflections over the finished image instead. `maxDistance` and `thickness` keep their names, `opacity` becomes `intensity`, and `selects` and `blur` have no settings.
entries.details: The material's roughness picks the surfaces and blurs their reflections, up to `maxRoughness`. A `groundReflector` (`ReflectorForSSRPass`) becomes a reflection pass, which wins on its plane. The `ssr()` node's `resolutionScale` becomes the `ssrScale` quality setting, which is 0 on the Low preset of phones. Its quality becomes `ssrSteps`, the most steps of each ray. Where a ray hits nothing on the screen, the environment's reflection shows.

entries.target: const pass = render.addPass({ kind: 'reflection', writes: 'water', plane: { point, normal } }); materials.shader({ wgsl, textures: { mirror: textures.fromPass(pass) } }), whose surface function sets s.reflection from reflection_uv
entries.notes: A reflection pass draws the camera's view mirrored across the plane, and an oblique near plane clips everything below it. The mesh no longer carries the reflection. A custom material reads the pass texture by screen position with `null3d::reflection::reflection_uv`, then sets the surface's reflection.
entries.details:
The texture's rows start at the top on the HDR WebGPU path, and `reflection_uv` turns the lookup there. `Reflector`'s `textureWidth` and `textureHeight` become `scale`, a share of the render size. Its color becomes the material's color with metalness 1 and roughness 0.

`Water`'s `distortionScale` becomes the factor on the normal's tilt in `reflection_uv`'s offset. `waterColor` becomes the material's color, and `sunColor` the scene's sun. `Water`'s normal map becomes ripples in the surface function. The reflection draws the scene's background, the sun's light and shadows, and the point and spot lights that it sees.

For a river or a lake, `createWater` from `@null3d/water` does this work. It adds the soft shore, the foam, the caustics and the view from under the water. A reflection pass stays the way to mirror a floor. For an open sea, `createOcean` from `@null3d/water` transforms wave spectra into the surface's heights and slopes on the GPU. `Refractor` and `Water2`'s refraction become transmission: give the water's custom material `transmission` and `thickness`. Its surface function sets `s.transmission` and its rippled normal.

entries.target: scene.setBackground({ sky: { sunPosition, turbidity, rayleigh, mieCoefficient, mieDirectionalG, cloudCoverage, ... } })
entries.notes: three.js's `Sky` works as the scene's background, with its uniforms' names, defaults and formulas, clouds and sun disc included. Drop the mesh and its scale: the sky draws behind every object. `SkyMesh` moves its clouds by the renderer's clock; pass the sketch's time as `time` instead.
entries.details:
The sky lights nothing, as in three.js. For its light, `scene.setEnvironment(await assets.skyEnvironment())` follows the sky in place of `pmremGenerator.fromScene`. `timeOfDay(hours)` gives a sky, a sun, fog and an exposure that match each other.

For a physical sky with ozone, twilight and haze on distant objects, move to `{ atmosphere }`. It looks different from three.js's sky. The default `sunPosition` is the sun of three.js's sky example, 2 degrees over the horizon toward -Z. It is not a `Sky` uniform default.

The sky is about 5 at the horizon by day, and three.js's sky examples use an exposure of 0.5. So a port lit by the sky's environment at full intensity looks brighter. Lower the environment's intensity or the exposure.

entries.three: A physical sky and aerial perspective (add-ons such as @takram/three-atmosphere: SkyMaterial, AerialPerspectiveEffect)
entries.target: scene.setBackground({ atmosphere: { sunPosition, sunIntensity, rayleigh, haze, ozone, aerialPerspective, metersPerUnit, moonPosition, moonIntensity, stars, cloudCoverage, ... } })
entries.notes: The engine's own physical sky comes from Hillaire's lookup tables, with no files to load. One background call draws the sky and hazes every object by its distance, so drop the sky mesh and its textures. Set `metersPerUnit` to the scene's scale, and `aerialPerspective` above 1 to make a small scene look larger.
entries.details: The sun's light is in the units of a directional light. Aim the scene's light at the sun yourself, or take it from `timeOfDay(hours, { model: 'physical' })`. The sky lights nothing by itself: `scene.setEnvironment(await assets.skyEnvironment())` follows it. The Low preset draws the analytic sky in its place. No separate aerial perspective effect is needed.

entries.target: Screen-space sprites placed with camera.worldToScreen

entries.three: GammaCorrectionShader / sRGB conversion passes in the composer
entries.target: Delete: output is converted to sRGB exactly once
entries.notes: Keeping such a pass applies gamma twice and washes the image out.

entries.target: await scene.createSprites({ count, map, atlas, sizeAttenuation, center })
entries.notes: Camera-facing quads draw in one batch, with typed arrays of positions, sizes, rotations, colors and atlas frames per sprite. The call is async, because the first one downloads the sprite code. Sprites blend by default, as three.js's do.
entries.details:
Without size attenuation, sizes are in CSS pixels, not a fraction of the view's height. A three.js scale s shows `s × h / (2 × tan(fov / 2))` CSS pixels on a canvas h CSS pixels high. `center` holds one value for the whole batch, not one per sprite. An atlas read through `texture.offset` and `texture.repeat` becomes `atlas` and `frames`.

`alphaTest` becomes `alphaMode 'mask'` with `alphaCutoff`. Raycasts hit each sprite's quad, as `Raycaster` does, with the active camera in place of `raycaster.camera`. `sprites.on('click', fn)` takes pointer events, and the event's `instance` is the sprite.

entries.target: await scene.createPoints({ positions, colors, size, sizeAttenuation, map })
entries.notes: Points of one size draw in one batch as camera-facing squares, at any size on every backend. The call is async, because the first one downloads the sprite code. Points are opaque by default, as three.js's are; `transparent` becomes `alphaMode 'blend'`, and `alphaMap` has no counterpart.
entries.details:
`alphaTest` becomes `alphaMode 'mask'` with `alphaCutoff`. With size attenuation, `size` is in world units: three.js's size times `tan(fov / 2)`. Without it, size is in CSS pixels, as in three.js. A point does not vanish when its center leaves the screen, as a WebGL point does. Blended points sort back to front.

Raycasts hit each point's square by default. The `pointThreshold` option gives `Raycaster.params.Points.threshold`'s test instead: a hit within that distance of the point, whatever its size. `points.on('click', fn)` takes pointer events, and the event's `instance` is the point. The geometry's position and color attributes become `positions` and `colors`.

With an orthographic camera, three.js ignores size attenuation, so port with `sizeAttenuation: false` and three.js's size. three.js's WebGPU renderer draws points one pixel wide, and WebGL lets a GPU cap their size as low as 1 pixel.

entries.three: Line / LineSegments / LineLoop / LineBasicMaterial / LineDashedMaterial / Line2 / LineSegments2 / LineMaterial
entries.target: await scene.createLines({ positions, colors, mode, width, worldUnits, dashed })
entries.notes: Segments between points draw in one batch as quads with round ends, as `Line2` draws them, at any width on every backend. `mode` replaces the line classes, and `width` replaces `linewidth`. The call is async, and `LineMaterial.resolution` needs no setting.
entries.details:
`'segments'` also replaces `LineSegments2` with `LineSegmentsGeometry`. A one-pixel `Line` ports as `width` 1. Point colors are linear RGB, stored at 8 bits per channel. `positions` replaces `LineGeometry.setPositions` or the position attribute, and `colors` replaces `setColors` or the color attribute.

`dashed` and the dash values replace `LineDashedMaterial` and `computeLineDistances`. `dashed` is fixed when the batch is created, and `lines.material.set` changes the four dash values, whose defaults match `LineMaterial`'s. `lit: true` shades lines with the scene's lights.

Raycasts hit a segment within half its width, as `Line2` does, in pixels through the active camera or in world units. The `lineThreshold` option gives `Raycaster.params.Line.threshold`'s test instead, as for `Line`. `maxDistance` limits line hits too, though three.js's `Line2` ignores `raycaster.far`. `lines.on('click', fn)` takes pointer events, and the event's `instance` is the segment.

entries.three: Points or InstancedMesh particles moved on the CPU / three.quarks ParticleSystem / three-nebula
entries.target: await createParticles(ctx, { rate, bursts, lifetime, shape, speed, gravity, drag, wind, turbulence, size, colors, alphaOverLife, blending, map, flipbook }) from @null3d/particles; system.update() in onLateUpdate
entries.notes: three.js has no particle system. A port replaces the loop that moves `Points` or `InstancedMesh` rows with an emitter whose particles the GPU moves in closed form. Gravity, drag toward the wind, turbulence and a bouncing ground come from options.
entries.details: Write the effect's look as curves over life in place of per-frame color and size code. `AdditiveBlending` becomes `blending 'additive'`; particles never write depth. A sprite atlas becomes `map` with `flipbook`. three.quarks's sub-emitters become `subEmitters` on `'death'` or `'ground'`. A system does not sort its own particles, cast shadows or take light.

entries.three: A PlaneGeometry displaced on the CPU, with heights from ImprovedNoise or a height map
entries.target: createTerrain(ctx, { size, height, layers, splat, maxLevel, camera }) from @null3d/terrain; terrain.update(eye) in onUpdate; terrain.heightAt(x, z)
entries.notes: A port replaces one displaced grid with a height field drawn as a camera-centered quadtree of blocks. The ground near the camera keeps fine detail, and the far hills draw coarse blocks. A skirt around each block hides the seam between neighbors more than one level apart.
entries.details:
Up to four tiled layers blend by a splat map. The add-on fills the map by default from the height and the slope, in place of a hand-painted or vertex-colored ground. Each layer's own height pushes it through its neighbors at a boundary. Every pixel lights from normals baked over the whole ground, so the far hills keep their relief.

The terrain carries no collision. A port that walked on the ground reads `heightAt` and `normalAt` to place objects instead of a physics collider. A port that morphed between levels drops its own morph. Each block morphs toward its parent block's surface before it hands over, so the ground does not pop. `morph: false` switches each block at once.

entries.three: A tree model per species loaded from a glTF file, or a procedural plant from an add-on such as Sapling or ez-tree, swaying in a custom wind shader
entries.target: const tree = await assets.loadGltf(url); scene.createInstances(tree.find(name).mesh, count, { material }) for the copies of each species; a materials.shader material whose vertexOffset samples the field of createWind(ctx, { camera }) from @null3d/wind, with swayDistance; far copies as cards from @null3d/impostors, with handOverToCards(meshes, cards.batch, switchDistance)
entries.notes: null3D ships no plant generator, so a port keeps its tree models. Export a procedural tree from Blender's Sapling, ez-tree or a similar tool as a glTF file, or build the tree in code. Draw each species' copies as one instance batch, so the engine gives them levels of detail and culling.
entries.details: For wind, replace the three.js shader's sway with one custom material whose vertex offset reads the wind add-on's field, as `api/wind` shows. The sway fades to nothing at the material's `swayDistance`, so far trees stand still and keep their cached shadows. Past the last level, cards from the impostors add-on stand in for the trees, and `handOverToCards` sets the two distance bands.

entries.target: Sketch: ui.trackLabel(obj, 'hp-12', { offset: [0, 2, 0] }). Page: engine.labels.bind('hp-12', element). A plane of the scene: ui.trackLabel(obj, 'card', { transform: 'world' }), or 'billboard' with a rotation
entries.notes: The sketch places each label with the camera of each frame, and the page moves the element over it in the frame on screen. The element's center sits where `CSS2DRenderer` puts a `CSS2DObject`'s, and the offset turns and scales with the object. The engine has no camera view offset.
entries.details:
Put the elements in a container that covers the canvas. Hidden labels get `visibility: hidden`, not `display: none`. There is no z-index by distance, and no center. Give an element `pointer-events: auto` for the clicks that `CSS3DRenderer` gives it.

For `CSS3DRenderer`, a label with `transform 'world'` takes a `CSS3DObject`'s matrix. `'billboard'` takes a `CSS3DSprite`'s, with `rotation2D` as `rotation`. The page moves the element into a container inside its parent, which holds the camera's perspective. It then turns the element with its world matrix, as `CSS3DRenderer` draws it. An element is sized in CSS pixels, which are the scene's units. Both perspective and orthographic cameras carry the planes, so a scene that uses either lens ports as it is.

The engine hides a plane whose anchor is behind the camera or outside the near and far planes. `CSS3DRenderer` does not do that. The offset follows the object as a `CSS2DObject`'s position does under its parent. The engine leaves the pointer to your CSS. It writes a transform only when it changes, and a page holds its planes with `maxLabels3d`.

All seven of three.js's CSS3D examples have a port: css3d_periodictable, css3d_molecules, css3d_sprites, css3d_sandbox, css3d_orthographic, css3d_mixed and css3d_youtube. Three also draw WebGL content: mixed, sandbox and orthographic. Where the mixed example's invisible plane writes depth alone to show its embedded page clean, a material with `colorWrite: false` does the same.

A cell table ports directly: one object and one `ui.trackLabel(object, id, { transform: 'world' })` for each cell. The cell's HTML goes in the element, and the example's camera. The port skill's architecture guide shows it.

entries.three: A field of grass blades as an InstancedMesh or a custom shader that bends them in a time-based wind
entries.target: await createGrass(ctx, { height, area, count, seed, mask, wind, camera, swayDistance }) from @null3d/grass, with grass.setWindLayer(field) in each frame to bend the blades in the wind add-on's field, grass.fit(preset) for a preset's share and grass.setSwayDistance(swayDistanceFor(preset)) when the preset changes
entries.notes: three.js has no grass. A port replaces the hand-made blades and their wind shader with one call. The add-on places the tufts on the ground's height by integer hash, so one seed places the same grass on every device.
entries.details: The add-on bends the blades in the wind add-on's field, so the grass answers the same gusts as the rest of the scene. On WebGPU a compute pass builds the blade list each frame, culls it to the view and thins the far tufts. WebGL2 draws the same rows as an instance batch. The grass casts and receives the sun's shadows. A blade shape, a width along the blade and the fold of its keel, takes the place of a hand-made blade geometry.

entries.target: const splats = await createSplats(ctx, { url }) from @null3d/splats; assets.loadGltf for a KHR_gaussian_splatting model
entries.notes: Importing `@null3d/splats` registers the `KHR_gaussian_splatting` reader, so a glTF model of splats loads with `assets.loadGltf`. An SPZ file loads through `createSplats`, which cuts the cloud into detail levels. It chooses the splats within a budget that follows the quality preset and the GPU path, then lets the engine sort them by depth.
entries.details: A large cloud loads as a splat stream: `createSplats` reads an index of chunk files and downloads only the chunks that the view needs. The cloud then draws before its whole file arrives. three.js has no equivalent. Update them once in each frame with `splats.update(eye)`, from the camera's `getPosition`. The first spherical-harmonic band gives each splat's color; higher bands are ignored. three.js's `GaussianSplat` and its loaders are add-ons, so each name maps to this one add-on.

entries.target: @null3d/sound: createSound in the sketch, connectSound on the page
entries.notes: `AudioListener` is `createSound`'s listener option, usually the camera. A looping `PositionalAudio` is a `sound.loop` at a place, with `refDistance` as `near`; one that plays once per event is a `sound.shot`. `AudioLoader` and `AudioAnalyser` have no counterpart: name the file by its address, and analyze the page's own Web Audio.
entries.details: three.js's `maxDistance` only stops the fall with distance, while `far` fades the sound out. Give `far` where the sound should end. A non-positional `Audio` is a loop with `positional: false`. The page loads the named file once the user starts the sound.

entries.three: React Three Fiber / drei (Canvas, useFrame, useGLTF, OrbitControls, Environment, Html)
entries.target: React stays for the page UI; the scene moves into sketch.ts
entries.notes: React keeps the page UI and talks to the sketch through messages. Rewrite each scene component and drei helper by hand. drei's `<Html>` becomes `ui.trackLabel` in the sketch, and `ContactShadows` and `onPointerMissed` have no counterpart.
entries.details:
The directional light's contact shadows are another technique in place of `ContactShadows`, a blurred shadow on a ground plane. Mesh events such as `onClick` and `onPointerEnter` become `obj.on('click')` and `obj.on('pointerenter')`.

React Three Fiber casts only against objects with handlers, and passes an event to every hit until `stopPropagation`. null3D passes it to the closest drawn object and its parents, so an object without handlers in front takes it. React Three Fiber's `onClick` also fires after a drag. null3D gives no click after a drag past 2 CSS pixels, or 10 for a finger. For a pointer miss, set a flag in click handlers, and treat `input.wasReleased('Mouse0')` without it as a miss.

entries.target: `plugins: [null3d()]` in vite.config.ts, with `null3d` imported from `@null3d/vite-plugin`
entries.notes: Every Vite build of a null3D project needs the plugin, for the dev server and for production, which a three.js project does not. It sends the headers that let worker threads share memory, compiles the WGSL, and builds the engine's workers. null3D supports Vite alone, so a project on another bundler moves to Vite.

entries.target: runTask: the task's module and its WebAssembly run in the engine's job workers
entries.notes: An add-on starts no worker of its own. Give `runTask` the address of a module that exports `run`, and await its answer. A `SharedArrayBuffer` in the task's input is shared with the worker rather than copied.
entries.details: The engine never waits for a task in a frame, and an answer arrives between frames.
